CABG. While CABG is an effective intervention for coronary atherosclerotic heart disease, perioperative neurological complications, particularly strokes, remain common and pose substantial risks to patients, their families and healthcare systems. Studies found the incidence of AIS during CABG ranging from 1.1% to 5.7%. In patients with severe CAS undergoing coronary surgery, stroke rates range from 3% to 11%. In our study, the incidence of new brain lesions in patients with moderate-to-severe CAS after CABG was 21.8%, which exceeds the previously reported studies. This highlights the role of low-field MRI and suggests that previous studies may have underestimated the incidence of postoperative stroke. Moreover, the brain lesions, such as silent ones, were associated with poor clinical outcomes including delirium, dementia and cognitive decline. This may impact perioperative management strategies and long-term care pathways, promote closer neurological follow-up and require further exploration in the future. Multiple factors contributed to postoperative new brain lesions. Although multivariable analysis did not demonstrate a significant correlation between the types and number of vascular stenosis and new brain lesions, a culprit stenosis vessel can be identified in about 2/3 patients appearing with new brain lesions. We suggest that the type and number of stenoses alone may not reliably indicate risk. Consistent with previous studies, our findings indicate a significant association between prolonged operative time and the development of new brain lesions. A growing body of evidence has identified extended CPB duration as an independent risk factor for postoperative stroke. In our analysis, patients who experienced postoperative stroke had significantly longer median CPB durations (165.5 min vs 136.0 min) and aortic cross-clamp durations (112.0 min vs 89.0 min) compared with those without stroke (p<0.001). Notably, among patients undergoing aortic dissection repair, the median CPB time was 185.0 min in the stroke group compared with 156.0 min in the non-stroke group (p=0.014). Furthermore, the risk of postoperative stroke increased significantly when CPB time exceeded 140.0 min. This association is likely related to haemodilution, intraoperative hypotension, inflammatory responses and the formation of microemboli during prolonged CPB. Both new brain lesions and the CABG procedure were significant contributors to cognitive decline. Population-based studies have shown a strong association between silent brain lesions and cognitive decline or dementia. Barber et al reported that cognitive decline in patients undergoing cardiac valve surgery was linked to postoperative ischaemic brain lesions. However, the impact of silent brain injuries on POCD remains controversial. In the study by Tachibana et al , POCD was common in patients with multiple and larger lesions, which may contribute to decreased ability to perform activities of daily living postoperatively and reduce long-term quality of life. They did not find an association between new brain lesions and MoCA or Mini–Mental State Examination scores after surgery. Our findings are not consistent with those in the study by Tachibana et al , in that we did not find differences in the impact of larger vs smaller lesions on cognitive decline. However, new brain lesions were an independent risk factor that is strongly associated with POCD, especially orientation ability. Furthermore, among the 71 patients without brain lesions, 12 (16.9%) showed cognitive decline. We suggested the procedure was associated with cognitive decline. Our study also found when LVEF was ≤55%, the specificity for predicting cognitive decline was 79.9%, although the sensitivity was lower. Heart failure is frequently associated with cognitive impairment, with some studies indicating that cognitive function is lower in patients with heart failure than in the general population. One contributing factor is that reduced cardiac output and episodes of hypotension can exacerbate cerebral hypoperfusion, particularly affecting regions critical for cognition. Additionally, perioperative stressors, including CPB, haemodynamic instability, hypoxia, microemboli and inflammation, further exacerbate cognitive decline. For example, CPB triggers cerebral hypoperfusion and embolic events, while systemic inflammation promotes neuroinflammation via cytokines like IL-1β and IL-18, linked to blood–brain barrier disruption and neuronal damage. According to our study, we suggest the patients with concomitant cerebrovascular stenosis are at high risk and require enhanced postoperative screening and perioperative management to prevent cognitive impairment. This study has several limitations. First, it was a single-centre retrospective analysis with a small sample size, limiting the generalisability of the findings. Selection bias may be present, as critically ill patients and those unable to complete cognitive or imaging assessments were excluded. Second, postoperative cognitive evaluations were conducted at 5–7 days after surgery, a period during which transient factors such as anaemia, hypoxia or anaesthetic effects may impact cognitive performance. Third, the short-time cognitive assessments may introduce a learning effect, especially as alternate versions of the MoCA in Chinese were unavailable. Fourth, we did not include detailed intraoperative parameters (eg, anaesthetic depth or haemodynamic fluctuations), which may influence neurological outcomes. Fifth, although cerebral small vessel disease is closely related to cognitive decline, our imaging evaluation was limited to Fazekas scoring. Other markers

those unable to complete cognitive or imaging assessments were excluded. Second, postoperative cognitive evaluations were conducted at 5–7 days after surgery, a period during which transient factors such as anaemia, hypoxia or anaesthetic effects may impact cognitive performance. Third, the short-time cognitive assessments may introduce a learning effect, especially as alternate versions of the MoCA in Chinese were unavailable. Fourth, we did not include detailed intraoperative parameters (eg, anaesthetic depth or haemodynamic fluctuations), which may influence neurological outcomes. Fifth, although cerebral small vessel disease is closely related to cognitive decline, our imaging evaluation was limited to Fazekas scoring. Other markers such as microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis were not assessed due to the limitations of low-field MRI. Sixth, while duplex ultrasound was used for vascular assessment based on the guideline support, its diagnostic accuracy is relatively limited compared with CTA or high-resolution MRI. Future studies should consider multimodal imaging to comprehensively evaluate cerebrovascular status. Finally, cognitive assessments were restricted to the short perioperative period; longer-term follow-up is needed to evaluate the persistence of cognitive changes. Conclusions Low-field MRI detected new brain lesions in 24 (21.8%) of patients after CABG. Both postoperative new brain lesions and CABG operative were significant contributors to cognitive decline. New brain lesions were strongly associated with cognitive decline, especially orientation ability. Future RCTs incorporating comprehensive neuropsychological assessments are warranted to validate these findings.

documents.title: ESVS 2024 Clinical practice guidelines on the management of abdominal aortic aneurysms

chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) has been associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD), including myocardial infarction (MI) and stroke; – however, existing studies are subject to several shortcomings. The relevant body of literature mainly comprises either 1) population based studies, which are substantially underpowered with regards to women and non-White populations, or 2) clinical studies that examine outcomes following AAA related intervention, typically endovascular or open surgical repair. , , – Notably, the latter frequently do not include comparison groups, or include as comparison groups patients with AAA who do not undergo AAA related intervention. – As such, results afford limited applicability to the general population to compare risk of adverse CVD outcomes among persons with and without AAA, especially after statistical adjustment for peri-operative cardiovascular risk. Existing longitudinal studies of individuals with AAA also may not have follow up periods of sufficient length to fully describe the most meaningful CVD risk endpoints. Additionally, an increasing number of relevant studies have employed the composite endpoint of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), generally, although not universally, defined to include MI, stroke, and all cause death. , Use of this endpoint alone has the potential to obscure which, if any, of its underlying components may disproportionately contribute to outcomes among patients with AAA. Against this background, an improved understanding of the contemporary risk of CVD among individuals with AAA is needed. With a maximum follow up of > 30 years and a study population that includes over 3 700 men and women self identifying as Black, data from the community based, prospective Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study can help address important gaps in the literature regarding AAA and cardiovascular outcomes. Moreover, a significant majority of AAA cases in ARIC were ascertained either incidentally during the course of an individual’s care or through clinical manifestation of AAA symptoms, rather than through population screening at an arbitrary time point. Therefore, ARIC data have the potential to allow for a more pragmatic longitudinal study of CVD risk following AAA diagnosis compared with existing studies. Findings may help inform management of cardiovascular risk factors among patients with AAA, which remains an area of inconsistency among major clinical practice guidelines. , METHODS Study population The ARIC study was a prospective cohort study of 15 792 adult participants recruited between 1987 and 1989 from four United States communities: Washington County, Maryland; Jackson, Mississippi; Suburban Minneapolis, Minnesota; and Forsyth County, North Carolina. , The ARIC study participants were followed for incident clinical AAA, and 5 911 surviving participants additionally underwent abdominal ultrasound screening for AAA at visit 5 (2011 – 2013). The ARIC study design and procedures have been described previously. , Of the 15 792 participants attending the ARIC baseline visit, 912 had experienced MI or stroke before visit 1, and 11 had previously undergone surgery for AAA and were therefore excluded from the present analysis. The following participants were also excluded: those with missing data for one or more study covariable(s) ( n = 620); those who self identified as of race other than Black or White ( n = 48); and those with an AAA diagnosis solely ascertained via a death certificate ( n = 8). Multiple exclusion criteria were met for 26 participants. These exclusions resulted in a final analytical sample of 14 219 individuals, as described in . Ascertainment of abdominal aortic aneurysm, outcomes, and covariables Clinical event follow up data through to 2021 were obtained for all ARIC participants who attended visit 1. Participants from Jackson, Mississippi, were followed through to 31 December 2020, due to difficulty obtaining hospital records in the region. The ARIC surveillance protocols led to the identification of both AAA and CVD related hospitalisation events and deaths. Hospitalisations were identified through regular telephone calls with study participants (annually before 2012, twice yearly thereafter), surveillance of hospital discharge lists in communities from which the ARIC participants were recruited, and linkage to state and national death registries. For participants who died, interviews were conducted with proxies whenever possible. International Classification of Diseases (ICD, revisions 9 and 10) Clinical Modification (CM) diagnostic discharge codes were recorded for all hospitalisations. AAA was ascertained in alignment with previously described ARIC study protocols. , ARIC surveillance procedures were used to ascertain AAA for all participants aged < 65 years. In addition, for participants aged > 65 years, linkage was performed with Medicare data from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to identify AAA. A clinical AAA diagnosis was defined as an ICD-9-CM code of either 441.3 or 441.4, or ICD-10-CM code I71.3 or I71.4. Incident surgical repair of AAA (defined as an ICD-9 procedure code 38.44 or ICD-10 procedure code 04Q00ZZ) or endovascular repair (defined as an ICD-9 procedure code 39.71 or ICD-10 procedure codes 04Q03ZZ or 04Q04ZZ) was identified in

protocols. , ARIC surveillance procedures were used to ascertain AAA for all participants aged < 65 years. In addition, for participants aged > 65 years, linkage was performed with Medicare data from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to identify AAA. A clinical AAA diagnosis was defined as an ICD-9-CM code of either 441.3 or 441.4, or ICD-10-CM code I71.3 or I71.4. Incident surgical repair of AAA (defined as an ICD-9 procedure code 38.44 or ICD-10 procedure code 04Q00ZZ) or endovascular repair (defined as an ICD-9 procedure code 39.71 or ICD-10 procedure codes 04Q03ZZ or 04Q04ZZ) was identified in a similar fashion, along with incident AAA rupture (defined as a new ICD-9-CM code 441.3 or ICD-10-CM code I71.3). In addition, 5 778 surviving ARIC participants underwent screening ultrasound to detect asymptomatic AAA at visit 5 (2011 – 2013). Screening ultrasound was performed by a trained cardiac ultrasonographer and imaging was reviewed by a radiologist with vascular expertise. AAA was diagnosed for any participant with an infrarenal aortic diameter ≥ 3 cm at any point. The primary outcomes were incident MI, incident stroke (both ischaemic and haemorrhagic), all cause death, and MACE (defined here as a composite of MI, stroke, and all cause death). Consistent with previously described ARIC study protocols, incident stroke and MI were ascertained via the relevant ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes and adjudicated by ARIC study physicians using medical records and death certificates. , Incident stroke and MI were defined as the first stroke or MI, respectively, diagnosed from visit 1 through to 2021 (or 2020, in the case of participants from Jackson, Mississippi). , Other variables collected at study baseline included participants’ demographic (age, race, sex, ARIC study site, and education level) and clinical characteristics (smoking status, pack years of smoking, and body mass index [BMI]). Laboratory tests were obtained, including high density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, low density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, total cholesterol, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), as well as pulmonary function tests (forced expiratory volume divided by forced vital capacity [FEV1/FVC], % predicted). Examined comorbidities included hypertension, use of antihypertensive medications, diabetes, peripheral artery disease (PAD), use of lipid lowering medications, and use of aspirin. Hypertension and PAD were ascertained according to ARIC study measurements of blood pressure and single leg ankle brachial index (ABI). Hypertension was captured using a continuous variable for systolic blood pressure. PAD was defined as an ABI < 0.90 for men or ABI < 0.85 for women. Diabetes was ascertained based on study measurements of serum glucose (fasting glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL or non-fasting glucose ≥ 140 mg/dL), participant self report of physician diagnosis, or use of diabetic medications in the preceding two weeks. Use of lipid lowering, antihypertensive, or diabetic medications and aspirin were ascertained according to participant self report and verified by an in person inventory. All participants provided informed consent, and institutional review board approval was obtained for the study. Data analysis Baseline clinical history and clinical and demographic characteristics were summarised by exposure category (incident AAA vs . non-AAA occurrence during follow up). Cumulative incidence and corresponding confidence intervals were calculated using the normal approximation to the Poisson distribution. For the primary analysis, multivariable Cox regression was used to estimate the association between incident clinical AAA (modelled as a time dependent variable) and subsequent risk of MI, stroke, all cause death, and MACE. Study covariables were modelled as time fixed variables, measured at baseline (visit 1) only. Participants who were not diagnosed with AAA during follow up contributed person time to the non-AAA group until death, CVD outcome, loss to follow up, or administrative censoring on 31 December 2021 (31 December 2020 for Jackson, Mississippi). Participants who were diagnosed with AAA during follow up contributed person time to the non-AAA group until the date of AAA diagnosis, and then to the AAA group thereafter until censoring occurred due to death, CVD outcome, loss to follow up, or administrative censoring on 31 December 2021 (31 December 2020 for Jackson, Mississippi). Participants whose CVD outcome(s) occurred before AAA diagnosis contributed person time to the non-AAA group only until the outcome occurred, at which point they were censored. The association between AAA and each outcome was analysed adjusting for two sets of covariables measured at visit 1. Firstly, a demographic adjusted model was created, accounting for age at baseline, sex, race, and ARIC field centre. A fully adjusted model was then created, adjusting for these same covariables as well as education level, BMI, height, smoking status, pack years of smoking, systolic blood pressure, eGFR, FEV1/FVC (% predicted), total cholesterol, LDL and HDL cholesterols, use of lipid lowering medications, use of aspirin, and diagnosis of peripheral artery disease and diabetes. Additionally, adjustment was made for AAA rupture and or open or endovascular AAA repair surgery that occurred before

adjusting for two sets of covariables measured at visit 1. Firstly, a demographic adjusted model was created, accounting for age at baseline, sex, race, and ARIC field centre. A fully adjusted model was then created, adjusting for these same covariables as well as education level, BMI, height, smoking status, pack years of smoking, systolic blood pressure, eGFR, FEV1/FVC (% predicted), total cholesterol, LDL and HDL cholesterols, use of lipid lowering medications, use of aspirin, and diagnosis of peripheral artery disease and diabetes. Additionally, adjustment was made for AAA rupture and or open or endovascular AAA repair surgery that occurred before the occurrence of a CVD outcome. Multiplicative interactions between AAA and smoking status, sex, and race were evaluated by including cross product terms in the fully adjusted models and testing for statistical significance. Interaction terms meeting criteria for statistical significance were included in the fully adjusted models. Analyses stratified by the interaction covariables were performed. Sensitivity analyses were conducted by excluding AAA cases detected via screening ultrasound at visit 5 (2011 – 2013), and separately by including updated potential confounders measured at study visit 4 (1996 – 1998), where available. Covariables measured at visit 4 included: smoking status, diabetes diagnosis, BMI, systolic blood pressure, eGFR, and use of aspirin, antihypertensive, and lipid lowering medications. This sensitivity analysis also included all of these covariables measured at visit 1, in addition to all other covariables measured at visit 1 from the original analysis. Updated covariables at visit 4 were not included for variables that were not expected to change (e.g., years of education) or variables that were not measured at visit 4 (e.g., FEV1/FVC and pack years of smoking). Updated visit 4 variables for which change from baseline was captured by other covariables were also not included in this sensitivity analysis (e.g., change in serum cholesterol levels is likely to correlate with change in BMI and use of lipid lowering medications). In addition, the competing risk of death was evaluated for MI and stroke using the Fine–Gray method to estimate subdistribution hazards. All analyses were performed using SAS 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA). RESULTS A total of 14 219 ARIC cohort participants who were probably free of AAA at visit 1 were included in the final analytical sample. Clinical and demographic characteristics of the study population are described in . On average, participants who developed AAA were 55.7 years old at visit 1 compared with 53.9 years for participants who remained free of AAA. The study population included 6 189 (44%) men and 8 030 (56%) women, with 3 707 participants (26%) identifying as Black and 10 512 (74%) identifying as White. During a mean follow up of 25.6 (SD 8.8) years, a new diagnosis of clinical AAA was recorded for 718 participants. Abdominal ultrasound screening conducted during ARIC visit 5 (2011 – 2013) identified 70 study participants with an AAA, of whom 47 were also diagnosed with clinical AAA after visit 5. A total of 741 study participants who had experienced an incident AAA between 1987 and 2021 (or 2020 for Jackson, Mississippi) were identified from the hospitalisation and ultrasound screening data, while 13 478 participants were free of AAA during that period. On average, incident AAA occurred 19.3 years (SD 7.55) after enrolment, when participants were on average 75.0 years old (SD 7.37). Participants in the AAA group had a mean follow up for all cause death of 25.9 (SD 6.9) years, including 6.9 (SD 5.9) years following an AAA diagnosis. Participants in the non-AAA group had a mean follow up time for all cause death of 25.5 years (SD 8.87). A total of 83 participants underwent open AAA repair, of whom nine had a diagnosis of ruptured AAA, while 76 underwent endovascular AAA repair, including three with a diagnosis of ruptured AAA. Unadjusted incidence rates of MI, stroke, all cause death, and MACE for ARIC participants with and without AAA, along with rate differences, are presented in . The incidence (95% CI) of MI per 1 000 person years among participants with AAA was 17.1 (17.0 – 17.2) compared with 5.4 (5.4 – 5.4) for participants without AAA, while incidence of stroke was 11.8 (11.7 – 11.9) among participants with AAA vs . 4.1 (4.1 – 4.1) for those without AAA. For participants with AAA, incidence of all cause death and MACE was 112.3 (112.0 – 112.6) and 122.7 (122.3 – 123.1), respectively, compared with 22.5 (22.5 – 22.6) and 27.1 (27.1 – 27.1), respectively, among participants without AAA. Hazard ratios associating AAA with respective outcomes of MI, stroke, death, and MACE are presented in , adjusted for potential confounding variables. In the fully adjusted model, comparing participants with and without incident AAA, the hazard ratio (95% CI) was 2.59 (1.34 – 5.03) for incident MI, 1.60

among participants with AAA vs . 4.1 (4.1 – 4.1) for those without AAA. For participants with AAA, incidence of all cause death and MACE was 112.3 (112.0 – 112.6) and 122.7 (122.3 – 123.1), respectively, compared with 22.5 (22.5 – 22.6) and 27.1 (27.1 – 27.1), respectively, among participants without AAA. Hazard ratios associating AAA with respective outcomes of MI, stroke, death, and MACE are presented in , adjusted for potential confounding variables. In the fully adjusted model, comparing participants with and without incident AAA, the hazard ratio (95% CI) was 2.59 (1.34 – 5.03) for incident MI, 1.60 (1.17 – 2.19) for stroke, 1.77 (1.58 – 1.99) for all cause death, and 2.18 (1.64 – 2.89) for MACE. The statistical significance of these hazard ratios at a pre-specified α of 0.05 was robust to sensitivity analysis, including only pragmatically ascertained AAA (i.e., excluding all AAA solely detected via screening ultrasound at visit 5) (data not presented). Significant interactions between AAA and sex were identified for the outcomes of MI, all cause death, and MACE, as well as between AAA and smoking status for the outcomes of MI and MACE ( and ). The hazard ratio (95% CI) for MI among women with AAA compared with those without AAA was 2.11 (1.28 – 3.48), which was greater than the hazard ratio of 1.32 (0.95 – 1.83) for MI among men with AAA compared with those without AAA ( p = .036). Similarly, the hazard ratios associated with the exposure of AAA for all cause death and MACE among women were 2.09 (1.75 – 2.49) and 2.11 (1.74 –2.57), respectively, compared with hazard ratios for men of 1.89 (1.68 – 2.13) and 1.87 (1.64 – 2.15) (interaction p = .025 for all cause death, interaction p = .007 for MACE), respectively. Moreover, the incidence rates of these outcomes were at least as high for women with AAA as men with AAA ( and ). Finally, the hazard ratios associated with AAA for the outcomes of MI and MACE were 1.57 (1.03 – 2.38) and 1.85 (1.57 – 2.17) among current smokers, 1.53 (0.94 – 2.47) and 2.10 (1.74 – 2.53) among former smokers, and 2.77 (1.43 – 5.37) and 2.40 (1.82 – 3.15) among never smokers (interaction p = .037 for MI, interaction p = .006 for MACE). No statistically significant interactions were detected between race and AAA. Results of sensitivity analysis including covariables updated at visit 4 are presented in , and selected participant characteristics measured at visit 4 are shown in . Adjusted hazard ratios associated with AAA for MI, stroke, death, and MACE all maintained statistical significance when selected covariables measured at visit 4 were included in the model ( ). The Fine–Gray subdistribution hazards for MI and stroke, accounting for the competing risk of death, were 2.62 ( p = .006) and 1.53 ( p = .007), respectively. DISCUSSION In this community based, prospective, cohort study with an average follow up of > 25 years, participants who developed clinical AAA had substantially higher incidence rates of CVD than those who did not develop AAA: namely, a 2.6 fold increased risk of MI, 1.6 fold increased risk of stroke, 1.8 fold increased risk of all cause death, and 2.2 fold increased risk of MACE. These associations were independent of the influence of cardiovascular risk factors at baseline, including demographic and clinical characteristics and relevant comorbid conditions, as well as excess CVD risk associated with aneurysm rupture and surgery to repair AAA. Moreover, the associations were demonstrated in a population that included previously understudied groups, namely women and people identifying as Black. The hazard ratios associating AAA with MI, all cause death, and MACE were higher for women than for men. In addition, the typically lower CVD incidence rate in women than men was eliminated in the presence of AAA ( and ). Regarding smoking, hazard ratios associating AAA with both MI and MACE were higher among never smokers, compared with former smokers and current smokers. Comparison with existing literature The results of this study add to the body of literature suggesting that AAA may represent an independent risk factor for CVD outcomes. , – The existing epidemiological literature, which includes several large population based studies, is summarised in and . In general, people with AAA have been shown to experience a significant excess mortality rate compared with the general population, and aortic diameter has been associated with both cardiovascular death and incident CVD events. , , , , The current findings, demonstrating a significantly increased risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes among people with AAA as compared with those free of AAA, are largely consistent with this body of literature. Similarly, the larger hazard ratio associating AAA with MI, all cause death, and MACE observed among women compared

literature, which includes several large population based studies, is summarised in and . In general, people with AAA have been shown to experience a significant excess mortality rate compared with the general population, and aortic diameter has been associated with both cardiovascular death and incident CVD events. , , , , The current findings, demonstrating a significantly increased risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes among people with AAA as compared with those free of AAA, are largely consistent with this body of literature. Similarly, the larger hazard ratio associating AAA with MI, all cause death, and MACE observed among women compared with men is broadly consistent with previous research demonstrating higher hazard ratios relating AAA to CVD outcomes among women compared with men. The higher hazard ratios for CVD outcomes observed among women compared with men in ARIC is largely due to the relatively low CVD rate in the hazard ratio comparison group of women vs . men without AAA. There are differences in magnitude of the association between AAA and CVD risk between the current results and those of comparable population based studies ( and ). For example, hazard ratios for MI (2.59) and MACE (2.18) in the ARIC population were substantially higher than the hazard ratio of 1.8 for MI and 1.79 for MACE observed in comparable studies. , Such differences may partly be attributed to the specific potential confounding variables accounted for in each analysis. The study conducted by Eldrup et al . included only people undergoing surgery for AAA in the exposure group, potentially excluding a large number of AAA not meeting criteria for surgical intervention. Similarly, both the National Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Screening Programme and Multi-Aneurysm Screening Study analyses included only men. , It is believed that the mean follow up time of approximately 26 years in the ARIC study population is the longest among comparable studies. Moreover, studies solely based on ultrasound screening probably identified less severe AAAs than ARIC, which mainly used hospitalised AAA as the exposure. Ascertainment of AAA in ARIC occurred between 1987 – 1989 and 2021, with most cases pragmatically ascertained over a long follow up of hospitalisations. By contrast, all relevant existing population based studies ascertained AAA via screening protocol performed either at a specific age or over a fixed time period. , , The mean age of ARIC participants upon study commencement was younger than that of the other studies, although the mean age at the time of AAA diagnosis was comparable with CHS. The proportion of participants identifying as Black (27.0%) and women (56.5%) in this study may be more representative of the population, potentially bolstering external validity. Clinical implications A significant shortfall in secondary prevention of adverse CVD outcomes has been reported for patients diagnosed with AAA. , The results of this study demonstrate that nearly half of participants who developed AAA were current smokers at visit 1, while the majority did not report use of cardiovascular risk reducing medications, including aspirin or a statin. However, further research is needed to investigate quality of care (or any gaps in care) for AAA patients in the ARIC study after their diagnosis. There are inconsistencies between major clinical practice guidelines with regards to strategies for cardiovascular risk factor reduction among patients with AAA. The 2024 European Society for Vascular Surgery guidelines recommend cardiovascular risk factor reduction in people with AAA, including blood pressure control and medical therapy with a statin and antiplatelet agent. By contrast, current American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines strongly recommend statin therapy in patients with AAA and evidence of atherosclerosis, but only weakly recommend consideration of antithrombotic therapy in patients with AAA. , The most recent Society for Vascular Surgery clinical practice guidelines recommend that patients undergoing AAA surveillance seek medical management for cardiovascular risk factors and specifically recommend consideration of a statin and ACE inhibitor for CVD risk reduction; however, no recommendation is made regarding aspirin or other antithrombotic therapy for these patients. These guideline discrepancies may partly reflect changing views of antiplatelet therapy for secondary prevention among people with AAA, with contemporary literature suggesting that the benefits of antiplatelet agents may be less significant than previously demonstrated. , , While the need for cardiovascular risk factor management is therefore acknowledged in contemporary clinical guidelines, the utility and importance of specific interventions remain areas of inconsistency. Moreover, existing evidence suggests that implementation of CVD prevention strategies, even where recommended, has been relatively neglected among patients with AAA. The current results suggest that the risk of CVD outcomes among people with AAA relative to the general population may be of greater magnitude than previously observed, adding urgency to recommendations for treatment of CVD risk factors as secondary prevention among people with AAA. Moreover, existing evidence suggests that implementation of CVD prevention strategies, even where recommended, has been relatively neglected among patients with AAA. The current results suggest that the risk of CVD outcomes among people with AAA relative to the general population may be of greater magnitude than previously observed, adding urgency to recommendations for treatment of CVD risk factors as secondary prevention among people with AAA. This is especially pertinent in the light of evidence suggesting that risk factor modification specifically including statin, antiplatelet, and antihypertensive therapy may improve overall survival in patients with a diagnosis of AAA. Strengths and limitations The mean follow up time of > 25 years represents an important strength of this study. However, major changes in clinical practice and guidelines for CVD prevention occurred during this extended follow up period. One weakness is that the present analysis may not reflect all aspects of current clinical care. For example, < 3% of participants reported use of a cholesterol lowering medication at visit 1, reflective of clinical practice in the period 1987 – 1989, but probably substantially lower than current levels. One possible strategy to address this could have involved use of time varying covariables, capturing changes during the study period. However, such an approach would have introduced selection bias, as covariables would only be updated when participants attended an ARIC study visit. Given the lower propensity of less healthy individuals to attend later study visits, this would have posed a substantial risk of differential misclassification. The sensitivity analysis including updated covariables at visit 4 yielded hazard ratios for all CVD outcomes associated with AAA that were equal or greater in magnitude than those observed in the primary analysis. While again noting the potential selection bias introduced by including these updated covariables at visit 4, results of this sensitivity analysis suggest that measuring covariables at visit 1 only may have biased the results towards the null. In addition, ascertainment of AAA based on hospital discharge codes may have biased the study findings in two ways. Firstly, hospitalisation based ascertainment of AAA may have preferentially identified more severe cases of AAA, which could have potentially inflated the measured association between AAA and CVD outcomes. Conversely, this approach may have failed to identify all AAA cases within the study population. While the screening ultrasound at study visit 5 probably captured many remaining asymptomatic AAA cases, not all study participants underwent ultrasound and it is likely that residual misclassification of AAA exposure is reflected in these results. Undiagnosed, subclinical AAA, if present in this study population, would have biased the results towards the null. Finally, this study compared outcomes among participants with AAA who began accruing person time later (at the time of AAA diagnosis) than participants without AAA. However, the risk of bias associated with this comparison was limited by statistical adjustment for baseline age in this model, as well as by the fact that incidence of MI, stroke, and death, as well as AAA, increases with age. Notably, such issues are not unique to the ARIC study, and do not strongly impact the comparison of these results with those of other longitudinal, population based studies. Conclusion This study provides evidence of a relationship between AAA and future risk of MI, stroke, and all cause death that is of equivalent or greater magnitude to that previously reported. Notably, the results demonstrate that this relationship persists over an extended follow up period, and within a sex balanced population that included a substantial proportion of participants identifying as Black. These results add urgency to recommendations for cardiovascular risk factor management among patients with a diagnosis of AAA. Supplementary Material MMC1 MMC2

chunks.content: Introduction Historical perspectives Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (rAAA) was first described in the 2nd century A.D. by the Greek physician Antyllus of Alexandria ( ). The description included a depiction of a patient with a pulsatile abdominal mass who subsequently developed severe abdominal pain and sudden death. Although AAAs have been present throughout human history, it was not until published results by Sir Astley Cooper in the 19th century on his experiences with treating patients with this condition that this disease came to the forefront of medical knowledge ( ). In fact, Cooper's writings provided Sir William Osler the necessary insights to further describe AAA patients by characterizing the clinical presentation, particularly the characteristic pulsatile abdominal mass and the propensity for rupture. In Osler's era, rare attempts at early diagnosis and surgical treatment were described, usually in the form of aortic ligation; however, mortality rates were exceedingly high ( ). As improved understanding of AAAs aligned with surgical innovation, by 1923, the first successful complete ligation of an aortic aneurysm was described. Notably, the patient survived for 17 months and subsequently died from tuberculosis ( ). Despite this landmark description, outcomes of aortic surgery remained dismal and a publication from the American Surgical Association in 1940 succinctly stated, “the results obtained by surgical intervention have been discouraging” ( , ). The modern era of rAAA management can be traced to the seminal contribution of Dr. Arthur Vorhees in 1951 ( ). He performed the first documented successful open AAA repair using an in-situ aorto-aortic bypass strategy with vinyon-N graft material (e.g., material used in parachutes!). This achievement catalyzed the “golden era” of aortic surgery with significant influences imparted by Debakey and Cooley ( , ). Although, the first case report of a successful repair of a ruptured AAA using Dacron graft was performed by Sutton in 1952, a number of technical improvements were made by Debakey, Cooley and subsequently Crawford from the 1950s to the 1970s. These included refinements in operative resuscitation, sequential clamp application, as well as selective visceral/lower extremity perfusion to mitigate the deleterious impact of ischemia-reperfusion sequelae perioperatively ( , ). Epidemiology and prevalence Although ruptured AAA is relatively uncommon compared to intact AAA, there are certain patient populations and geographic regions that have higher incidence and prevalence. It is estimated that 6%–8% of the population over age 60 have an AAA globally ( ). AAA is more commonly observed in older adults with an increasing risk among men ( , ). In fact, the prevalence for infrarenal AAAs is 4–5 fold higher for men compared to women and potentially amplified in the setting of a smoking history. Further, certain populations have higher rates of aneurysm disease especially among Northern European and North American nations which likely is influenced by genetic factors, as well as lifestyle choices (e.g., smoking) ( ). The overall prevalence for AAA in multiple population based studies ranges from 3%-5% in men aged 65–70 and exceeds 10% among subjects over the age of 80. Moreover, several reported risk factors are recognized to be important contributors to AAA morbidity ( , ). Notably, there is significant overlap among covariates that contribute both to AAA growth and rupture risk. The strongest predictors include smoking exposure (relative risk increases 3–5-fold) and family history (RR∼2-fold) ( ). Additional variables such as oxygen-dependent COPD, coronary artery disease, hypertension, cerebrovascular and peripheral artery disease, as well as mixed connective tissue disorders all have associations with the natural history of AAA ( ). Notwithstanding the impact of these other biologic factors that have been implicated in AAA morbidity, to date, diameter remains the single most important predictor that is used to inform perioperative rupture risk assessments. It is important to highlight that historical estimates for diameter-associated rupture risk are now recognized to have been overestimated since they were predominantly based on retrospective observations, as well as autopsy studies. This point is highlighted by the recently published North American Society for Vascular Surgery's updated guideline implementation document ( ). Specifically, a 5.5 cm diameter for a man now has an endorsed annualized rupture risk of −1%–3% (which is less than the −5%–6% that was commonly espoused previously). Similarly, a 6.0 cm AAA has an approximately 3%–6% risk of rupture per year which is roughly half of what was reported in historical guidelines and series ( ) ( ). These revised estimates may have clinical implications surrounding recommended diameter thresholds for surgical repair. These revised estimates may have clinical implications surrounding recommended diameter thresholds for surgical repair. Risk factors and screening Although the focus of this review is to highlight ruptured AAA management, an accounting of the relevant risk factors and further emphasis about the importance of population-based screening programs provides additional context to this discussion. The current understanding about the underlying etiology of degenerative AAA disease is characterized by a systemic process that impacts vessel wall biology leading to loss of important vascular structural proteins and strength ( ). In fact, the intersection of underlying predisposing genetic factors, inflammatory mediators and proteases underscores the development of aneurysm formation. However, certain exogenous factors including tobacco use (and by extension COPD), as well as hypertension are known to further exacerbate this process. Moreover, male sex preponderance (4–5:1 vs. female patients), increasing age, familial history (e.g., 1st degree relative), other peripheral aneurysms (e.g., iliac, femoral, popliteal), and atherosclerosis have all been recognized to be additional important risk factors for AAA development ( ). Optimal medical therapies in AAA patients include longitudinal judicious blood pressure management and complete smoking/nicotine abstinence given the known direct deleterious impact this exposure has on cytoskeletal biology in the extra-cellular matrix of the aorta. Further, the use of antiplatelet agents and statin therapies are helpful to reduce long-term cardiovascular risk but there are no known pharmacologic therapies that reduce AAA growth/rupture at this time ( ). Notably, the success of smoking cessation programs at a national level have led to a decline in AAA prevalence over time. Additionally, population-based screening programs in many countries around the world have successfully reduced AAA mortality in the past 20 years ( , ). Nationwide programs usually screen males ages 65–75 who have ever smoked and most suggest screening males aged 65–75 who have a first-degree relative who has been diagnosed with AAA. Selectively, screening can be offered to female patients who have a first-degree relative who has been diagnosed with AAA; however, screening is not otherwise indicated for women. Lastly, the Society for Vascular Surgery (SVS) and European Society for Vascular Surgery (ESVS) guidelines also suggest rescreening individuals at the 10-year time point if their original aortic diameter is between 2.5 and 3.0 cm ( , ). Evolution in patient management and procedure selection Early recognition and diagnosis Due to the sobering outcomes that are still reported for rAAA presentations, early diagnosis and treatment to either prevent overt rupture or rapidly triage patients with emergent symptoms remains a cornerstone of modern management. This philosophy has long been recognized to be a crucial component to the care of patients presenting non-electively with any number of acute aortic syndromes. Due to the need for timely diagnosis and treatment of the rAAA patient, emergency room providers need to have a high-index of suspicion for any patient within the 5th-9th decade of life that presents with abdominal or back pain with or without hemodynamic lability, syncope, flank/periumbilical ecchymosis and/or unexplained fall/loss of consciousness, etc. Further, any patient with a known history of AAA (either diagnosed previously or having a positive family history with first degree relatives), as well as subjects with known or suspected mixed connective tissue disease should also be considered high-risk for a rAAA presentation. This should prompt rapid acquisition of diagnostic imaging (e.g., FAST vs. CT angiography with CT being the gold standard) to rule out the possibility of an aortic emergency. In an effort to coordinate care and expediently transfer and/or treat rAAA, there are several descriptions of large healthcare networks that have successfully implemented ‘hub and spoke’ models to centralize care of these patients ( , ). The concept can be generally described as follows: once a smaller hospital or satellite emergency room has identified a patient to have a rAAA, there are clear process of care algorithms ( ) that are enacted similar to treatment of patients experiencing acute coronary syndromes or stroke. In fact, this strategy has been successfully employed in different regions of the United States, as well as multiple European and Australasian nations ( , ). The value of these protocol driven care pathways for rAAA patients is that it provides non-vascular health care practitioners with the necessary information to appropriately diagnose, notify, support and rapidly transfer patients to larger more complex tertiary referral “centers of excellence” for definitive management. Secular regionalization of rAAA care has occurred in North America; however, this unfortunately has not been uniform in its application ( ). Unlike Canadian, most European, and some Australasian nations that have single-payor systems that can mandate regionalization, a predominantly fee-for-service health ecosystem and an overriding doctrine to preserve both patient and

nations ( , ). The value of these protocol driven care pathways for rAAA patients is that it provides non-vascular health care practitioners with the necessary information to appropriately diagnose, notify, support and rapidly transfer patients to larger more complex tertiary referral “centers of excellence” for definitive management. Secular regionalization of rAAA care has occurred in North America; however, this unfortunately has not been uniform in its application ( ). Unlike Canadian, most European, and some Australasian nations that have single-payor systems that can mandate regionalization, a predominantly fee-for-service health ecosystem and an overriding doctrine to preserve both patient and physician autonomy has been associated with the unintended consequence of slowing centralization within the United States ( ). This distinction is somewhat ironic since the original description of a center volume association with postoperative outcome relationship after major cavitary and extirpative surgery was actually described by Luft and colleagues in 1979 from their analysis of patients treated in California ( ). Additional barriers to regionalization of rAAA management in the U.S. have included complex geographic, financial, and patient-related factors which has led to growing calls from professional societies to incentivize centralization models both in the U.S and internationally ( , , ). Despite this uneven adoption of rAAA care regionalization, the upstate New York experience highlights the successful implementation of a coordinated care network among 12 different hospitals ( ). For example, over a 13-year period, a multi-disciplinary protocol was derived through collaboration among surgeons, emergency room physicians, anesthesiologists, nurses and radiology technicians. Virtual platforms for image sharing, as well as resuscitative physiologic parameters were prospectively prescribed. Interestingly, the likelihood for exposure to a specific treatment strategy (e.g., open vs. EVAR) was vastly different depending on where the operation was performed (community hospital-94% open vs. university ‘hub’ hospital-38% open). More importantly, transferred patients, had significantly improved mortality outcomes compared to their community-treated rAAA counterparts (e.g., 30-day mortality: university open repair, 27% vs. community open repair, 46%) ( ). Although the difference among EVAR treated patients was less evident, there was still a strong trend toward improved morbidity, length of stay, and reintervention outcomes for the ‘hub’ hospital endovascular repairs compared to the referral network institutions. Interestingly, the results of this regional success in New York state has been demonstrated at the national level in several European countries further validating the success of this modern care model for rAAA ( ). Pre-hospital and emergency department management Current strategies that are now routinely employed for the pre-hospital and emergency department management of a rAAA are informed by lessons extrapolated from military and civilian trauma experiences. Modernization of trauma care delivery systems in the late 20th century included advances in the assessment and management of both blunt and penetrating trauma victims ( ). State of the art principles exported from trauma networks into rAAA care algorithms now include empiric application of supplemental oxygen, large bore intravenous access (e.g., bilateral antecubital fossa, 14–16 gauge), permissive hypotension (e.g., SBP 70–90 mmHg), restrictive isotonic crystalloid infusion, and (if available), occasionally external anti-shock garments ( ). Optimally, some permutation of a health information portability and accountability act (HIPAA)-compliant “aortic alert system” can be rapidly activated upon recognition and during the process of hospital transfer ( , , ). This notification alerts the on-call vascular surgeon, anesthesiologist, operating room team, blood bank personnel and critical care teams. Information including the patient name, age, intravenous access, hemodynamic status (including use of vasopressors and airway status), level of consciousness, pre-hospital cardiopulmonary resuscitation history, code status and estimated time of arrival are some of the fundamental components that are usually needed to transfer the patient to the appropriate level of care ( , , ). Evolution in patient selection Proper patient selection is crucial to all surgical endeavors and rAAA is no exception. Patients frequently present with advanced age and may have associated hemodynamic instability and profound metabolic derangements. Therefore, it is incumbent on both the referring and accepting physicians to have a clear understanding of not only the current physiologic status of the patient but also (if possible) some insight about the relevant medical history and patient/family goals of care. Optimally, emergency room providers should address goals of care with a patient and their family (assuming hemodynamic stability) to obviate unnecessary transfer, cost, and waste of important resources. There are anecdotal descriptions of modern health system integration with technology being leveraged in these situations ( ). The concept being that this would facilitate real-time accepting surgeon-to-patient phone conversation (e.g., “face time” or telehealth visit) as a way for the referral center to interact with the subject before transfer to ensure an attempt at rAAA repair along with all of the postoperative risk and potential sequelae are truly something they want to pursue. Although this sounds ideal, in reality, this rarely

There are anecdotal descriptions of modern health system integration with technology being leveraged in these situations ( ). The concept being that this would facilitate real-time accepting surgeon-to-patient phone conversation (e.g., “face time” or telehealth visit) as a way for the referral center to interact with the subject before transfer to ensure an attempt at rAAA repair along with all of the postoperative risk and potential sequelae are truly something they want to pursue. Although this sounds ideal, in reality, this rarely occurs since vascular surgeons managing rAAA patients are usually confronted with a complex multi-dimensional problem that requires rapid decision-making to arrive at an optimal treatment plan that often has to be enacted before the patient even arrives (e.g., operating room team preparing instrumentation, anesthesia-surgeon communication, ICU bed creation, etc.). Not surprisingly, a number of preoperative risk stratification tools (e.g., Glasgow Aneurysm Score, Hardman Index, VQI rAAA score, etc.) have been published to facilitate the clinical decision making between surgeons and patients with rAAA and quantify surgical risk in this tenuous cohort ( , , – ). Although none have been shown to be “optimal”, consideration of age, anatomic complexity (e.g., need for supra-mesenteric cross-clamp), pre-hospital hemodynamic instability and/or loss of consciousness have been consistently reported to be high-risk variables that reliably predict poor outcomes after rAAA repair. For example, Robinson and colleagues identified that rAAA patients with all 4 of these risk factors had a 90%–100% mortality outcome with attempted repair ( ). Similarly, the University of Washington rAAA risk score has been shown to be associated with >80% mortality if patients have age >76, SBP <70 mmHg at any time preoperatively, serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dl and serum pH <7.2 ( ) ( ). This identifies a subset of patients that should probably be considered futile and deemed inoperable. However, a majority of patients will have some constellation of different risk factors so risk-assessment tools alone should not supplant judgment of the operating surgeon. Moreover, despite numerous publications, the widespread adoption of these risk predictor adjuncts remains scant in daily practice. Imaging Some of the most important advancements in the modern management of rAAA can be linked to improvements and innovation in preoperative and intraoperative imaging. The gold-standard for imaging is thin-sliced (<1.0 mm) computed tomographic angiography with reformatted images ( ). Most modern healthcare systems across different nations now have access to these scanners and the authors consider it mandatory that patients have a CTA before arrival to the operating room. This remains true even in the hemodynamically unstable patient—since without appropriate imaging, the aneurysm extent, associated morphology, and assessment of the paravisceral aorta would be unknown. Blindly operating on a rAAA that was diagnosed using point-of-care ultrasound is not recommended especially since delineation of relevant anatomic characteristics informs the operating surgeon about the optimal treatment modality and surgical approach (e.g., open vs. endovascular repair; if open, retroperitoneal vs. transperitoneal, etc.). Rapid imaging acquisition times now permit obtaining this vital anatomic information with minimal delay toward operative repair. However, we concede that there are some centers ( ) who will allow patients with rAAA to proceed to the operating room without a CT scan and may achieve good results. Irrespective of what imaging bias is employed, an efficient care system is required to ensure timely delivery of the patient to the operating theater. Due to the increasing adoption of endovascular techniques to manage the entire spectrum of acute aortic syndromes, many high-volume centers routinely employ three dimensional modeling for rAAA patients using a number of different software platforms (e.g., Siemens Syngo.via®, Osirix ™ , 3Mensio Vascular®, or TeraRecon, Inc., etc.). Contemporary tertiary aortic referral centers commonly have their own cloud sharing services that allow referring hospitals to rapidly upload images while patients are being transferred. The accepting surgeon can then take these images, generate a 3D-model and determine anatomic eligibility for attempted endovascular repair. Moreover, this designation helps the operating room team so it can set-up the appropriate equipment and instrumentation. To further highlight advancements in imaging, modern care of the rAAA patient now increasingly utilizes fixed imaging suites that have on-table, real-time software to allow for hybridized CT-fusion imaging, as well as intravascular ultrasound that are useful adjunctive techniques that can often facilitate endovascular repair. The caveat being that the patient has enough hemodynamic stability and that the processes of care at the treating center efficiently employ these novel imaging tools without delaying definitive repair. Perioperative physiological management Hemodynamic support Initial resuscitation in the operating room immediately before repair should generally follow the philosophy highlighted previously in the preoperative phase.
