documents.title: ESVS arteriovenous fistula clinical practice guidelines for hemodialysis

chunks.content: Background Hemodialysis remains the most prevalent form of kidney replacement therapy [ ], and the native arteriovenous fistula (AVF) is still considered the gold standard for vascular access. Compared with central venous catheters, AVFs are associated with superior patency rates and improved patient survival [ ]. Following surgical creation of an anastomosis, abrupt changes in hemodynamic conditions induce adaptive vascular remodeling characterized by venous dilatation and wall thickening, aiming to re-establish physiological levels of intramural tensile stress and wall shear stress [ ]. However, this adaptive process is not universal. Aberrant inward stenotic remodeling may develop either early or late in the postoperative period, compromising AVF maturation or long-term patency [ ]. In AVFs, stenotic lesions are most commonly localized in the juxta-anastomotic segment, whereas in arteriovenous grafts (AVGs) they typically occur at the venous anastomosis or in the draining vein. Development of stenosis represents the principal cause of vascular access dysfunction and loss. Duplex ultrasound (DUS) is the first-line imaging modality for surveillance and diagnosis of vascular access complications and demonstrates diagnostic accuracy comparable to angiography [ ]. Significant venous stenosis is defined by a combination of morphological and functional DUS parameters, including luminal diameter reduction > 50%, a peak systolic velocity ratio > 2–3 and at least one additional criterion: residual diameter < 2 mm, reduced access flow < 500 mL/min for AVFs and < 600 mL/min for AVGs, or an access flow decrease > 25% when the previous flow was < 1000 mL/min [ , ]. However, these criteria are somewhat complex, require substantial operator experience, and may not always reliably identify stenoses that are likely to progress to access failure. Therefore, there is a continued clinical need for additional, simple and easily reproducible ultrasound parameters that may improve the detection of hemodynamically relevant stenoses and facilitate earlier intervention. In this case series, we describe an interesting ultrasound finding — a low-frequency, high-amplitude vessel wall flutter at the site of perianastomotic stenosis — observed in failing AVFs and discuss its potential value as an adjunctive sign for identifying clinically significant stenosis. Case presentations Case 1 A 72-year-old man with multiple cardiovascular comorbidities urgently initiated hemodialysis in May 2024 via a dialysis catheter. End-stage kidney disease (ESKD) was multifactorial, predominantly hypertensive and diabetic glomerulosclerosis with superimposed infection-associated glomerulonephritis. Following preoperative DUS mapping, a radiocephalic AVF was created with anastomosis at the junction of the distal and middle third of the right forearm. Early postoperative DUS demonstrated adequate maturation parameters with an access flow of approximately 700 mL/min and a fistula vein diameter of 5 mm. Cannulation was started three weeks after creation, because of catheter-related complications. Two months later, a DUS exam was repeated because of cannulation difficulties. It revealed a perianastomotic stenosis with a minimal luminal diameter of 1.9 mm, preserved flow of 670 mL/min, and associated vessel wall flutter at the exit from the stenotic segment (see Fig. and Supplementary Video ). At follow-up DUS four months later, access flow declined to 440 mL/min, prompting percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA) using a 4-mm drug-eluting balloon (DEB; see Fig. , panel C). Despite initial technical success, restenosis developed within five months, and a surgical reanastomosis was performed. Case 2 An 80-year-old woman with hypertensive and valvular cardiomyopathy and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction initiated chronic hemodialysis in December 2024. The etiology of ESKD was presumed to be chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis with secondary glomerulosclerosis. A radiocephalic AVF was constructed in the distal right forearm three months prior to dialysis initiation. After eight months of successful use, cannulation difficulties prompted DUS evaluation, which demonstrated an access flow of 450 mL/min and a perianastomotic stenosis with 1.1 mm residual lumen, accompanied by vessel wall flutter (see Fig. and Supplementary Video ). Surgical reanastomosis was performed two weeks later. A follow-up DUS performed six weeks after reanastomosis showed an improvement in flow to 700 mL/min, with a new perianastomotic stenosis due to vein kinking with 1.5 mm lumen, again with vessel wall flutter. The patient is scheduled for further follow-up DUS after three months. In the meantime, the AVF remains in regular use without complications. Case 3 A 66-year-old man with long-standing diabetes mellitus and multiple associated complications, including diabetic nephropathy, initiated chronic hemodialysis in 2019. A radiocephalic AVF at the right wrist, created two months earlier, failed to mature due to a perianastomotic stenosis, and subsequent surgical reanastomosis was also unsuccessful. An upper-arm AVG was subsequently created in the right arm in September 2020. After good initial function, the graft developed recurrent venous outflow stenoses and thromboses, which ultimately resulted in access abandonment, after multiple thrombectomies and PTAs. In September 2025, a new radiocephalic AVF was created in the distal left forearm. Six weeks postoperatively, DUS demonstrated a non-matured AVF: a low access flow of 250 mL/min, a perianastomotic stenosis

initiated chronic hemodialysis in 2019. A radiocephalic AVF at the right wrist, created two months earlier, failed to mature due to a perianastomotic stenosis, and subsequent surgical reanastomosis was also unsuccessful. An upper-arm AVG was subsequently created in the right arm in September 2020. After good initial function, the graft developed recurrent venous outflow stenoses and thromboses, which ultimately resulted in access abandonment, after multiple thrombectomies and PTAs. In September 2025, a new radiocephalic AVF was created in the distal left forearm. Six weeks postoperatively, DUS demonstrated a non-matured AVF: a low access flow of 250 mL/min, a perianastomotic stenosis of 1.4 mm and a marked vessel wall flutter (see Fig. and Supplementary Video ). PTA using a 4-mm DEB resulted in transient improvement in access flow to 550 mL/min, but AVF still could not be used regularly. One month later, DUS showed a reduced flow of 280 mL/min and recurrent stenosis with a luminal diameter of 1.5 mm. A second PTA using a 6-mm DEB improved flow to 470 mL/min and AVF was subsequently successfully used for dialysis. Discussion In all three cases presented, a visually apparent vessel wall flutter on DUS was consistently associated with anatomically and clinically relevant perianastomotic stenosis. In the first case, wall flutter was identified at a time when access flow was still preserved, preceding subsequent flow decline and AVF dysfunction. In the remaining two cases, wall flutter was observed in the presence of severely reduced luminal diameter, with either borderline or clearly reduced access flow, and prompted further intervention. In the second case, vessel wall flutter recurred after surgical reanastomosis, but this time due to kinking; and the patient is scheduled for close ultrasound follow-up to further evaluate the temporal evolution of this finding and its possible development into true stenosis. In the third case, wall flutter resolved after balloon angioplasty, despite borderline access flow, suggesting that disappearance of wall flutter may reflect a relevant improvement in local hemodynamics beyond simple luminal diameter or flow measurements, which are prone to measurement errors. Importantly, wall flutter was detected at the perianastomotic location in all three patients, indicating that this phenomenon reflects a localized hemodynamic disturbance rather than an incidental finding. Potential mechanism Two distinct types of vessel wall vibration phenomena should be differentiated. High-frequency wall vibrations in the range of several hundred hertz (Hz), previously described in fluid–structure interaction studies of AVFs, are attributed to turbulence-induced pressure fluctuations and are not directly detectable on routine clinical ultrasound imaging, as they are not visible with the naked eye [ – ]. In contrast, the visually apparent post-stenotic wall flutter observed in our cases occurred at a substantially lower frequency and involved the immediate post-stenotic dilated segment. The frequency was estimated at 1–2 Hz, corresponding to cardiac systole, with a relative wall motion of approximately a third of the maximal vessel diameter. The observed wall flutter is consistent with the well-described phenomenon of paradoxical systolic wall collapse [ ]. In a hemodynamically significant stenosis, marked flow acceleration occurs due to conversion of static pressure into kinetic energy, resulting in high flow velocities within and at the exit of the stenosis that promote flow instability and transitional flow, which is associated with high-frequency wall vibrations. A transient post-stenotic pressure drop may result in negative transmural pressure, causing vessel wall collapse or low-frequency, high-amplitude wall flutter, as observed in our cases. Turbulent flow components are present throughout this region, and higher-frequency oscillations likely coexist in the post-stenotic region. However, these are not visually discernible on standard ultrasound imaging. Wall flutter appears to preferentially occur at the distal end of the stenosis, where the vessel wall remains relatively compliant due to the absence of extensive intimal hyperplasia, allowing transient inward deformation and elastic recoil. The occurrence of wall collapse and flutter likely depends on stenosis severity, post-stenotic pressure reduction in the outflow vein, surrounding tissue pressure, and local wall properties, and have been described in cases of ≥ 70% stenosis [ ]. Vessel wall flutter likely has negative effects on the vessel wall itself and can cause vessel wall fatigue and resultant post-stenotic aneurysmatic dilatation [ ]. High-frequency oscillations, on the other hand, could be associated with stenosis development [ ]. Clinical implications The observation of visually apparent vessel wall flutter during routine ultrasound examination may have potential clinical implications, as it could be easier to recognize than standard diagnostic measures. For example, depending on image settings, a subtle intraluminal narrowing can be missed, especially when caused by intimal hyperplasia or thin venous valves. Furthermore, it is difficult to assess an increase in flow velocity in the perianastomotic region due to turbulence from the anastomosis. Wall motion assessment is also less dependent on high spatial resolution, needed to detect intimal hyperplasia, and optimal Doppler settings. As such, wall flutter

[ ]. Clinical implications The observation of visually apparent vessel wall flutter during routine ultrasound examination may have potential clinical implications, as it could be easier to recognize than standard diagnostic measures. For example, depending on image settings, a subtle intraluminal narrowing can be missed, especially when caused by intimal hyperplasia or thin venous valves. Furthermore, it is difficult to assess an increase in flow velocity in the perianastomotic region due to turbulence from the anastomosis. Wall motion assessment is also less dependent on high spatial resolution, needed to detect intimal hyperplasia, and optimal Doppler settings. As such, wall flutter may represent a simple and readily identifiable adjunctive ultrasound sign that raises suspicion for a hemodynamically significant stenosis, particularly in situations where access flow measurements remain borderline or Doppler assessment is limited by aliasing, tissue bruiting or signal saturation. The presence of wall flutter may therefore prompt closer DUS surveillance or further invasive diagnostic evaluation before overt access dysfunction develops. Limitations Assessment of wall flutter was primarily qualitative. It should be regarded as an adjunctive, hypothesis-generating visual sign rather than a validated diagnostic criterion. Accordingly, inter- or intra-observer variability was not formally evaluated. Although the phenomenon was independently recognised by several operators, examiner blinding and standardised measurement protocols were not employed. Quantitative estimates of frequency and wall displacement were derived retrospectively from a limited number of available ultrasound clips and should therefore be regarded as semi-quantitative and exploratory rather than standardized diagnostic thresholds. Apparent vessel wall motion on ultrasound may arise from alternative mechanisms, including transmitted arterial pulsatility, excessive probe pressure or high-flow states. In our cases, wall flutter was consistently localized to the immediate post-stenotic segment and was absent in adjacent non-stenotic venous segments examined using identical probe position and ultrasound settings. Transmitted arterial pulsatility was considered unlikely given the focal nature of the finding, its disappearance following stenosis-targeted intervention, and the fact that several ultrasound clips did not include the artery within the same imaging plane. Excessive probe pressure, particularly in the superficial perianastomotic region, represents a relevant potential source of false-positive wall deformation and should be carefully avoided. Furthermore, the occurrence of visually detectable wall flutter likely depends on specific anatomical and mechanical conditions, including focal stenosis severity, post-stenotic pressure reduction and preserved wall compliance. In near-critical or multiple sequential stenoses with extensive energy dissipation, as well as in noncompliant or excessively dilated veins, visually apparent wall flutter may be attenuated or absent. All reported cases involved perianastomotic stenosis in radiocephalic AVFs limiting generalizability to other anatomical locations and grafts. Larger prospective studies are required to determine the reproducibility, diagnostic accuracy and prognostic significance of vessel wall flutter as an ultrasound criterion associated with clinically relevant AVF stenosis. Conclusions In this exploratory case series, we describe a recurrent and visually apparent ultrasound finding — a low-frequency, high-amplitude vessel wall flutter — associated with hemodynamically relevant perianastomotic stenosis in failing arteriovenous fistulas. Wall flutter was observed before overt access flow reduction and resolved following effective intervention, suggesting that it may reflect changes in local hemodynamics not fully captured by luminal diameter or access flow measurements alone. As a dynamic and easily recognizable sign, vessel wall flutter may serve as a useful adjunctive ultrasound finding potentially associated with clinically significant AVF stenosis. Prospective studies are warranted to validate its diagnostic and prognostic value. Supplementary Information Below is the link to the electronic supplementary material. documents.title: ESVS guidelines on follow-up after vascular interventions

chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) has been associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD), including myocardial infarction (MI) and stroke; – however, existing studies are subject to several shortcomings. The relevant body of literature mainly comprises either 1) population based studies, which are substantially underpowered with regards to women and non-White populations, or 2) clinical studies that examine outcomes following AAA related intervention, typically endovascular or open surgical repair. , , – Notably, the latter frequently do not include comparison groups, or include as comparison groups patients with AAA who do not undergo AAA related intervention. – As such, results afford limited applicability to the general population to compare risk of adverse CVD outcomes among persons with and without AAA, especially after statistical adjustment for peri-operative cardiovascular risk. Existing longitudinal studies of individuals with AAA also may not have follow up periods of sufficient length to fully describe the most meaningful CVD risk endpoints. Additionally, an increasing number of relevant studies have employed the composite endpoint of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), generally, although not universally, defined to include MI, stroke, and all cause death. , Use of this endpoint alone has the potential to obscure which, if any, of its underlying components may disproportionately contribute to outcomes among patients with AAA. Against this background, an improved understanding of the contemporary risk of CVD among individuals with AAA is needed. With a maximum follow up of > 30 years and a study population that includes over 3 700 men and women self identifying as Black, data from the community based, prospective Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study can help address important gaps in the literature regarding AAA and cardiovascular outcomes. Moreover, a significant majority of AAA cases in ARIC were ascertained either incidentally during the course of an individual’s care or through clinical manifestation of AAA symptoms, rather than through population screening at an arbitrary time point. Therefore, ARIC data have the potential to allow for a more pragmatic longitudinal study of CVD risk following AAA diagnosis compared with existing studies. Findings may help inform management of cardiovascular risk factors among patients with AAA, which remains an area of inconsistency among major clinical practice guidelines. , METHODS Study population The ARIC study was a prospective cohort study of 15 792 adult participants recruited between 1987 and 1989 from four United States communities: Washington County, Maryland; Jackson, Mississippi; Suburban Minneapolis, Minnesota; and Forsyth County, North Carolina. , The ARIC study participants were followed for incident clinical AAA, and 5 911 surviving participants additionally underwent abdominal ultrasound screening for AAA at visit 5 (2011 – 2013). The ARIC study design and procedures have been described previously. , Of the 15 792 participants attending the ARIC baseline visit, 912 had experienced MI or stroke before visit 1, and 11 had previously undergone surgery for AAA and were therefore excluded from the present analysis. The following participants were also excluded: those with missing data for one or more study covariable(s) ( n = 620); those who self identified as of race other than Black or White ( n = 48); and those with an AAA diagnosis solely ascertained via a death certificate ( n = 8). Multiple exclusion criteria were met for 26 participants. These exclusions resulted in a final analytical sample of 14 219 individuals, as described in . Ascertainment of abdominal aortic aneurysm, outcomes, and covariables Clinical event follow up data through to 2021 were obtained for all ARIC participants who attended visit 1. Participants from Jackson, Mississippi, were followed through to 31 December 2020, due to difficulty obtaining hospital records in the region. The ARIC surveillance protocols led to the identification of both AAA and CVD related hospitalisation events and deaths. Hospitalisations were identified through regular telephone calls with study participants (annually before 2012, twice yearly thereafter), surveillance of hospital discharge lists in communities from which the ARIC participants were recruited, and linkage to state and national death registries. For participants who died, interviews were conducted with proxies whenever possible. International Classification of Diseases (ICD, revisions 9 and 10) Clinical Modification (CM) diagnostic discharge codes were recorded for all hospitalisations. AAA was ascertained in alignment with previously described ARIC study protocols. , ARIC surveillance procedures were used to ascertain AAA for all participants aged < 65 years. In addition, for participants aged > 65 years, linkage was performed with Medicare data from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to identify AAA. A clinical AAA diagnosis was defined as an ICD-9-CM code of either 441.3 or 441.4, or ICD-10-CM code I71.3 or I71.4. Incident surgical repair of AAA (defined as an ICD-9 procedure code 38.44 or ICD-10 procedure code 04Q00ZZ) or endovascular repair (defined as an ICD-9 procedure code 39.71 or ICD-10 procedure codes 04Q03ZZ or 04Q04ZZ) was identified in

protocols. , ARIC surveillance procedures were used to ascertain AAA for all participants aged < 65 years. In addition, for participants aged > 65 years, linkage was performed with Medicare data from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to identify AAA. A clinical AAA diagnosis was defined as an ICD-9-CM code of either 441.3 or 441.4, or ICD-10-CM code I71.3 or I71.4. Incident surgical repair of AAA (defined as an ICD-9 procedure code 38.44 or ICD-10 procedure code 04Q00ZZ) or endovascular repair (defined as an ICD-9 procedure code 39.71 or ICD-10 procedure codes 04Q03ZZ or 04Q04ZZ) was identified in a similar fashion, along with incident AAA rupture (defined as a new ICD-9-CM code 441.3 or ICD-10-CM code I71.3). In addition, 5 778 surviving ARIC participants underwent screening ultrasound to detect asymptomatic AAA at visit 5 (2011 – 2013). Screening ultrasound was performed by a trained cardiac ultrasonographer and imaging was reviewed by a radiologist with vascular expertise. AAA was diagnosed for any participant with an infrarenal aortic diameter ≥ 3 cm at any point. The primary outcomes were incident MI, incident stroke (both ischaemic and haemorrhagic), all cause death, and MACE (defined here as a composite of MI, stroke, and all cause death). Consistent with previously described ARIC study protocols, incident stroke and MI were ascertained via the relevant ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes and adjudicated by ARIC study physicians using medical records and death certificates. , Incident stroke and MI were defined as the first stroke or MI, respectively, diagnosed from visit 1 through to 2021 (or 2020, in the case of participants from Jackson, Mississippi). , Other variables collected at study baseline included participants’ demographic (age, race, sex, ARIC study site, and education level) and clinical characteristics (smoking status, pack years of smoking, and body mass index [BMI]). Laboratory tests were obtained, including high density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, low density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, total cholesterol, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), as well as pulmonary function tests (forced expiratory volume divided by forced vital capacity [FEV1/FVC], % predicted). Examined comorbidities included hypertension, use of antihypertensive medications, diabetes, peripheral artery disease (PAD), use of lipid lowering medications, and use of aspirin. Hypertension and PAD were ascertained according to ARIC study measurements of blood pressure and single leg ankle brachial index (ABI). Hypertension was captured using a continuous variable for systolic blood pressure. PAD was defined as an ABI < 0.90 for men or ABI < 0.85 for women. Diabetes was ascertained based on study measurements of serum glucose (fasting glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL or non-fasting glucose ≥ 140 mg/dL), participant self report of physician diagnosis, or use of diabetic medications in the preceding two weeks. Use of lipid lowering, antihypertensive, or diabetic medications and aspirin were ascertained according to participant self report and verified by an in person inventory. All participants provided informed consent, and institutional review board approval was obtained for the study. Data analysis Baseline clinical history and clinical and demographic characteristics were summarised by exposure category (incident AAA vs . non-AAA occurrence during follow up). Cumulative incidence and corresponding confidence intervals were calculated using the normal approximation to the Poisson distribution. For the primary analysis, multivariable Cox regression was used to estimate the association between incident clinical AAA (modelled as a time dependent variable) and subsequent risk of MI, stroke, all cause death, and MACE. Study covariables were modelled as time fixed variables, measured at baseline (visit 1) only. Participants who were not diagnosed with AAA during follow up contributed person time to the non-AAA group until death, CVD outcome, loss to follow up, or administrative censoring on 31 December 2021 (31 December 2020 for Jackson, Mississippi). Participants who were diagnosed with AAA during follow up contributed person time to the non-AAA group until the date of AAA diagnosis, and then to the AAA group thereafter until censoring occurred due to death, CVD outcome, loss to follow up, or administrative censoring on 31 December 2021 (31 December 2020 for Jackson, Mississippi). Participants whose CVD outcome(s) occurred before AAA diagnosis contributed person time to the non-AAA group only until the outcome occurred, at which point they were censored. The association between AAA and each outcome was analysed adjusting for two sets of covariables measured at visit 1. Firstly, a demographic adjusted model was created, accounting for age at baseline, sex, race, and ARIC field centre. A fully adjusted model was then created, adjusting for these same covariables as well as education level, BMI, height, smoking status, pack years of smoking, systolic blood pressure, eGFR, FEV1/FVC (% predicted), total cholesterol, LDL and HDL cholesterols, use of lipid lowering medications, use of aspirin, and diagnosis of peripheral artery disease and diabetes. Additionally, adjustment was made for AAA rupture and or open or endovascular AAA repair surgery that occurred before

A fully adjusted model was then created, adjusting for these same covariables as well as education level, BMI, height, smoking status, pack years of smoking, systolic blood pressure, eGFR, FEV1/FVC (% predicted), total cholesterol, LDL and HDL cholesterols, use of lipid lowering medications, use of aspirin, and diagnosis of peripheral artery disease and diabetes. Additionally, adjustment was made for AAA rupture and or open or endovascular AAA repair surgery that occurred before the occurrence of a CVD outcome. Multiplicative interactions between AAA and smoking status, sex, and race were evaluated by including cross product terms in the fully adjusted models and testing for statistical significance. Interaction terms meeting criteria for statistical significance were included in the fully adjusted models. Analyses stratified by the interaction covariables were performed. Sensitivity analyses were conducted by excluding AAA cases detected via screening ultrasound at visit 5 (2011 – 2013), and separately by including updated potential confounders measured at study visit 4 (1996 – 1998), where available. Covariables measured at visit 4 included: smoking status, diabetes diagnosis, BMI, systolic blood pressure, eGFR, and use of aspirin, antihypertensive, and lipid lowering medications. This sensitivity analysis also included all of these covariables measured at visit 1, in addition to all other covariables measured at visit 1 from the original analysis. Updated covariables at visit 4 were not included for variables that were not expected to change (e.g., years of education) or variables that were not measured at visit 4 (e.g., FEV1/FVC and pack years of smoking). Updated visit 4 variables for which change from baseline was captured by other covariables were also not included in this sensitivity analysis (e.g., change in serum cholesterol levels is likely to correlate with change in BMI and use of lipid lowering medications). In addition, the competing risk of death was evaluated for MI and stroke using the Fine–Gray method to estimate subdistribution hazards. All analyses were performed using SAS 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA). RESULTS A total of 14 219 ARIC cohort participants who were probably free of AAA at visit 1 were included in the final analytical sample. Clinical and demographic characteristics of the study population are described in . On average, participants who developed AAA were 55.7 years old at visit 1 compared with 53.9 years for participants who remained free of AAA. The study population included 6 189 (44%) men and 8 030 (56%) women, with 3 707 participants (26%) identifying as Black and 10 512 (74%) identifying as White. During a mean follow up of 25.6 (SD 8.8) years, a new diagnosis of clinical AAA was recorded for 718 participants. Abdominal ultrasound screening conducted during ARIC visit 5 (2011 – 2013) identified 70 study participants with an AAA, of whom 47 were also diagnosed with clinical AAA after visit 5. A total of 741 study participants who had experienced an incident AAA between 1987 and 2021 (or 2020 for Jackson, Mississippi) were identified from the hospitalisation and ultrasound screening data, while 13 478 participants were free of AAA during that period. On average, incident AAA occurred 19.3 years (SD 7.55) after enrolment, when participants were on average 75.0 years old (SD 7.37). Participants in the AAA group had a mean follow up for all cause death of 25.9 (SD 6.9) years, including 6.9 (SD 5.9) years following an AAA diagnosis. Participants in the non-AAA group had a mean follow up time for all cause death of 25.5 years (SD 8.87). A total of 83 participants underwent open AAA repair, of whom nine had a diagnosis of ruptured AAA, while 76 underwent endovascular AAA repair, including three with a diagnosis of ruptured AAA. Unadjusted incidence rates of MI, stroke, all cause death, and MACE for ARIC participants with and without AAA, along with rate differences, are presented in . The incidence (95% CI) of MI per 1 000 person years among participants with AAA was 17.1 (17.0 – 17.2) compared with 5.4 (5.4 – 5.4) for participants without AAA, while incidence of stroke was 11.8 (11.7 – 11.9) among participants with AAA vs . 4.1 (4.1 – 4.1) for those without AAA. For participants with AAA, incidence of all cause death and MACE was 112.3 (112.0 – 112.6) and 122.7 (122.3 – 123.1), respectively, compared with 22.5 (22.5 – 22.6) and 27.1 (27.1 – 27.1), respectively, among participants without AAA. Hazard ratios associating AAA with respective outcomes of MI, stroke, death, and MACE are presented in , adjusted for potential confounding variables. In the fully adjusted model, comparing participants with and without incident AAA, the hazard ratio (95% CI) was 2.59 (1.34 – 5.03) for incident MI, 1.60

among participants with AAA vs . 4.1 (4.1 – 4.1) for those without AAA. For participants with AAA, incidence of all cause death and MACE was 112.3 (112.0 – 112.6) and 122.7 (122.3 – 123.1), respectively, compared with 22.5 (22.5 – 22.6) and 27.1 (27.1 – 27.1), respectively, among participants without AAA. Hazard ratios associating AAA with respective outcomes of MI, stroke, death, and MACE are presented in , adjusted for potential confounding variables. In the fully adjusted model, comparing participants with and without incident AAA, the hazard ratio (95% CI) was 2.59 (1.34 – 5.03) for incident MI, 1.60 (1.17 – 2.19) for stroke, 1.77 (1.58 – 1.99) for all cause death, and 2.18 (1.64 – 2.89) for MACE. The statistical significance of these hazard ratios at a pre-specified α of 0.05 was robust to sensitivity analysis, including only pragmatically ascertained AAA (i.e., excluding all AAA solely detected via screening ultrasound at visit 5) (data not presented). Significant interactions between AAA and sex were identified for the outcomes of MI, all cause death, and MACE, as well as between AAA and smoking status for the outcomes of MI and MACE ( and ). The hazard ratio (95% CI) for MI among women with AAA compared with those without AAA was 2.11 (1.28 – 3.48), which was greater than the hazard ratio of 1.32 (0.95 – 1.83) for MI among men with AAA compared with those without AAA ( p = .036). Similarly, the hazard ratios associated with the exposure of AAA for all cause death and MACE among women were 2.09 (1.75 – 2.49) and 2.11 (1.74 –2.57), respectively, compared with hazard ratios for men of 1.89 (1.68 – 2.13) and 1.87 (1.64 – 2.15) (interaction p = .025 for all cause death, interaction p = .007 for MACE), respectively. Moreover, the incidence rates of these outcomes were at least as high for women with AAA as men with AAA ( and ). Finally, the hazard ratios associated with AAA for the outcomes of MI and MACE were 1.57 (1.03 – 2.38) and 1.85 (1.57 – 2.17) among current smokers, 1.53 (0.94 – 2.47) and 2.10 (1.74 – 2.53) among former smokers, and 2.77 (1.43 – 5.37) and 2.40 (1.82 – 3.15) among never smokers (interaction p = .037 for MI, interaction p = .006 for MACE). No statistically significant interactions were detected between race and AAA. Results of sensitivity analysis including covariables updated at visit 4 are presented in , and selected participant characteristics measured at visit 4 are shown in . Adjusted hazard ratios associated with AAA for MI, stroke, death, and MACE all maintained statistical significance when selected covariables measured at visit 4 were included in the model ( ). The Fine–Gray subdistribution hazards for MI and stroke, accounting for the competing risk of death, were 2.62 ( p = .006) and 1.53 ( p = .007), respectively. DISCUSSION In this community based, prospective, cohort study with an average follow up of > 25 years, participants who developed clinical AAA had substantially higher incidence rates of CVD than those who did not develop AAA: namely, a 2.6 fold increased risk of MI, 1.6 fold increased risk of stroke, 1.8 fold increased risk of all cause death, and 2.2 fold increased risk of MACE. These associations were independent of the influence of cardiovascular risk factors at baseline, including demographic and clinical characteristics and relevant comorbid conditions, as well as excess CVD risk associated with aneurysm rupture and surgery to repair AAA. Moreover, the associations were demonstrated in a population that included previously understudied groups, namely women and people identifying as Black. The hazard ratios associating AAA with MI, all cause death, and MACE were higher for women than for men. In addition, the typically lower CVD incidence rate in women than men was eliminated in the presence of AAA ( and ). Regarding smoking, hazard ratios associating AAA with both MI and MACE were higher among never smokers, compared with former smokers and current smokers. Comparison with existing literature The results of this study add to the body of literature suggesting that AAA may represent an independent risk factor for CVD outcomes. , – The existing epidemiological literature, which includes several large population based studies, is summarised in and . In general, people with AAA have been shown to experience a significant excess mortality rate compared with the general population, and aortic diameter has been associated with both cardiovascular death and incident CVD events. , , , , The current findings, demonstrating a significantly increased risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes among people with AAA as compared with those free of AAA, are largely consistent with this body of literature. Similarly, the larger hazard ratio associating AAA with MI, all cause death, and MACE observed among women compared

In general, people with AAA have been shown to experience a significant excess mortality rate compared with the general population, and aortic diameter has been associated with both cardiovascular death and incident CVD events. , , , , The current findings, demonstrating a significantly increased risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes among people with AAA as compared with those free of AAA, are largely consistent with this body of literature. Similarly, the larger hazard ratio associating AAA with MI, all cause death, and MACE observed among women compared with men is broadly consistent with previous research demonstrating higher hazard ratios relating AAA to CVD outcomes among women compared with men. The higher hazard ratios for CVD outcomes observed among women compared with men in ARIC is largely due to the relatively low CVD rate in the hazard ratio comparison group of women vs . men without AAA. There are differences in magnitude of the association between AAA and CVD risk between the current results and those of comparable population based studies ( and ). For example, hazard ratios for MI (2.59) and MACE (2.18) in the ARIC population were substantially higher than the hazard ratio of 1.8 for MI and 1.79 for MACE observed in comparable studies. , Such differences may partly be attributed to the specific potential confounding variables accounted for in each analysis. The study conducted by Eldrup et al . included only people undergoing surgery for AAA in the exposure group, potentially excluding a large number of AAA not meeting criteria for surgical intervention. Similarly, both the National Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Screening Programme and Multi-Aneurysm Screening Study analyses included only men. , It is believed that the mean follow up time of approximately 26 years in the ARIC study population is the longest among comparable studies. Moreover, studies solely based on ultrasound screening probably identified less severe AAAs than ARIC, which mainly used hospitalised AAA as the exposure. Ascertainment of AAA in ARIC occurred between 1987 – 1989 and 2021, with most cases pragmatically ascertained over a long follow up of hospitalisations. By contrast, all relevant existing population based studies ascertained AAA via screening protocol performed either at a specific age or over a fixed time period. , , The mean age of ARIC participants upon study commencement was younger than that of the other studies, although the mean age at the time of AAA diagnosis was comparable with CHS. The proportion of participants identifying as Black (27.0%) and women (56.5%) in this study may be more representative of the population, potentially bolstering external validity. Clinical implications A significant shortfall in secondary prevention of adverse CVD outcomes has been reported for patients diagnosed with AAA. , The results of this study demonstrate that nearly half of participants who developed AAA were current smokers at visit 1, while the majority did not report use of cardiovascular risk reducing medications, including aspirin or a statin. However, further research is needed to investigate quality of care (or any gaps in care) for AAA patients in the ARIC study after their diagnosis. There are inconsistencies between major clinical practice guidelines with regards to strategies for cardiovascular risk factor reduction among patients with AAA. The 2024 European Society for Vascular Surgery guidelines recommend cardiovascular risk factor reduction in people with AAA, including blood pressure control and medical therapy with a statin and antiplatelet agent. By contrast, current American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines strongly recommend statin therapy in patients with AAA and evidence of atherosclerosis, but only weakly recommend consideration of antithrombotic therapy in patients with AAA. , The most recent Society for Vascular Surgery clinical practice guidelines recommend that patients undergoing AAA surveillance seek medical management for cardiovascular risk factors and specifically recommend consideration of a statin and ACE inhibitor for CVD risk reduction; however, no recommendation is made regarding aspirin or other antithrombotic therapy for these patients. These guideline discrepancies may partly reflect changing views of antiplatelet therapy for secondary prevention among people with AAA, with contemporary literature suggesting that the benefits of antiplatelet agents may be less significant than previously demonstrated. , , While the need for cardiovascular risk factor management is therefore acknowledged in contemporary clinical guidelines, the utility and importance of specific interventions remain areas of inconsistency. Moreover, existing evidence suggests that implementation of CVD prevention strategies, even where recommended, has been relatively neglected among patients with AAA. The current results suggest that the risk of CVD outcomes among people with AAA relative to the general population may be of greater magnitude than previously observed, adding urgency to recommendations for treatment of CVD risk factors as secondary prevention among people with AAA. Moreover, existing evidence suggests that implementation of CVD prevention strategies, even where recommended, has been relatively neglected among patients with AAA. The current results suggest that the risk of CVD outcomes among people with AAA relative to the general population may be of greater magnitude than previously observed, adding urgency to recommendations for treatment of CVD risk factors as secondary prevention among people with AAA. This is especially pertinent in the light of evidence suggesting that risk factor modification specifically including statin, antiplatelet, and antihypertensive therapy may improve overall survival in patients with a diagnosis of AAA. Strengths and limitations The mean follow up time of > 25 years represents an important strength of this study. However, major changes in clinical practice and guidelines for CVD prevention occurred during this extended follow up period. One weakness is that the present analysis may not reflect all aspects of current clinical care. For example, < 3% of participants reported use of a cholesterol lowering medication at visit 1, reflective of clinical practice in the period 1987 – 1989, but probably substantially lower than current levels. One possible strategy to address this could have involved use of time varying covariables, capturing changes during the study period. However, such an approach would have introduced selection bias, as covariables would only be updated when participants attended an ARIC study visit. Given the lower propensity of less healthy individuals to attend later study visits, this would have posed a substantial risk of differential misclassification. The sensitivity analysis including updated covariables at visit 4 yielded hazard ratios for all CVD outcomes associated with AAA that were equal or greater in magnitude than those observed in the primary analysis. While again noting the potential selection bias introduced by including these updated covariables at visit 4, results of this sensitivity analysis suggest that measuring covariables at visit 1 only may have biased the results towards the null. In addition, ascertainment of AAA based on hospital discharge codes may have biased the study findings in two ways. Firstly, hospitalisation based ascertainment of AAA may have preferentially identified more severe cases of AAA, which could have potentially inflated the measured association between AAA and CVD outcomes. Conversely, this approach may have failed to identify all AAA cases within the study population. While the screening ultrasound at study visit 5 probably captured many remaining asymptomatic AAA cases, not all study participants underwent ultrasound and it is likely that residual misclassification of AAA exposure is reflected in these results. Undiagnosed, subclinical AAA, if present in this study population, would have biased the results towards the null. Finally, this study compared outcomes among participants with AAA who began accruing person time later (at the time of AAA diagnosis) than participants without AAA. However, the risk of bias associated with this comparison was limited by statistical adjustment for baseline age in this model, as well as by the fact that incidence of MI, stroke, and death, as well as AAA, increases with age. Notably, such issues are not unique to the ARIC study, and do not strongly impact the comparison of these results with those of other longitudinal, population based studies. Conclusion This study provides evidence of a relationship between AAA and future risk of MI, stroke, and all cause death that is of equivalent or greater magnitude to that previously reported. Notably, the results demonstrate that this relationship persists over an extended follow up period, and within a sex balanced population that included a substantial proportion of participants identifying as Black. These results add urgency to recommendations for cardiovascular risk factor management among patients with a diagnosis of AAA. Supplementary Material MMC1 MMC2

documents.title: ESVS clinical practice guidelines on management of abdominal aorto-iliac artery aneurysms

chunks.content: Background Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) represents a significant vascular disorder characterized by permanent, localized dilation of the abdominal aorta, typically defined as a diameter exceeding 3.0 cm or measuring 1.5 times the normal adjacent aortic segment , ( ). Anatomically, approximately 80% of AAAs occur inferior to the renal arteries (infrarenal), with remaining cases classified as suprarenal or pararenal based on their relationship to renal vessels. , True aneurysms, the most common form, involve dilation of all three arterial wall layers, while pseudoaneurysms result from arterial injury leading to blood extravasation between wall layers. Morphologically, AAAs typically demonstrate fusiform (circumferential) expansion, though saccular (asymmetric) variants occasionally occur. The clinical significance of AAA lies in its propensity for progressive, often asymptomatic expansion until the catastrophic complication of rupture occurs, carrying mortality rates exceeding 80%. Contemporary epidemiological data reveal a substantial decline in AAA prevalence compared to historical estimates, reflecting significant public health achievements in risk factor modification. Recent large-scale screening programs demonstrate that AAA prevalence among 65-year-old men has decreased from 1.32% to 0.69% between 2010 and 2023 in population-based cohorts. General population imaging studies using CT angiography report current prevalence rates of 4.0% in men versus 0.7% in women, maintaining the well-established male predominance with approximately 5-6-fold higher disease burden in males. , Meta-analyses of contemporary screening data demonstrate pooled odds ratios of 3.78 (95% CI 2.80–5.10) for male sex as a risk factor for AAA. These figures represent a remarkable reduction from the historical 4–8% prevalence range reported in earlier screening programs, primarily attributed to declining smoking rates and enhanced cardiovascular risk management in high-income countries. , Global mortality patterns reflect similar improvements, with age-standardized mortality rates declining from 2.57 to 1.86 per 100,000 between 1992 and 2021 (estimated annual percentage change −1.36%), though absolute deaths have increased due to population aging. Significant regional disparities persist, with age-adjusted mortality in US adults aged 65+ declining dramatically from 32.6 to 13.2 per 100,000 between 1999 and 2020, while high-income Asia Pacific regions maintain among the highest age-standardized death rates at 4.38 per 100,000. , These favorable trends contrast with stable or increasing AAA burdens reported in some Eastern European and lower Socio-demographic Index (SDI) regions, highlighting substantial geographic heterogeneity in AAA epidemiology and underscoring ongoing healthcare disparities that require targeted intervention strategies. , The natural history of AAA progression demonstrates substantial heterogeneity that complicates clinical management. Contemporary studies report means expansion rates of 2.16–2.6 mm/year with considerable individual variability. , While baseline diameter independently predicts growth velocity, it explains only minimal interpatient variability (R 2 = 0.054), highlighting the limitation of size-based monitoring alone. This variability is particularly evident in sex-specific analyses, where size-stratified analyses in women reveal mean annual growth rates of 0.91 mm/year for aneurysms <3.0 cm, 2.34 mm/year for 3.0–3.9 cm, 2.49 mm/year for 4.0–4.9 cm, and 6.16 mm/year for aneurysms ≥5.0 cm, demonstrating accelerating expansion with increasing diameter. Imaging characteristics provide crucial prognostic information beyond simple diameter measurements. The presence of intraluminal thrombus (ILT) doubles expansion rates (median 2.0 vs 1.0 mm/year), especially in smaller aneurysms. Growth patterns further stratify risk, with “peak growth” trajectories conferring a 5.24-fold higher hazard (95% CI 1.68–16.38) of requiring surgical intervention within one year compared to “edge growth” patterns. Contemporary surveillance data reveal that baseline diameter strongly influences intervention timing, with no patients measuring <4.25 cm requiring repair within two years, compared to 26% of those with baseline diameters ≥4.25 cm. The limitations of diameter-based risk assessment become particularly evident in rupture prediction. Recent biomechanical studies demonstrate that peak wall stress and rupture index independently predict rupture risk after adjusting for diameter. Among patients who experienced rupture, the median maximum diameter was 56 mm at last imaging, with median time to rupture of 2.13 years (IQR 0.64–4.72), confirming that catastrophic events occur near conventional intervention thresholds. Rupture continues to carry devastating consequences, with overall fatality exceeding 80% and 30-day hospital mortality ranging from 16–36% in contemporary series. , These observations collectively underscore the critical need for advanced biomarkers and personalized risk prediction tools that integrate biomechanical parameters, growth patterns, and molecular signatures to improve patient outcomes beyond current diameter-dependent paradigms. The pathophysiology of AAA involves a complex interplay of chronic inflammation, extracellular matrix degradation, vascular smooth muscle cell apoptosis, and oxidative stress. , These processes are orchestrated by intricate signaling networks that remain incompletely understood. Current management remains predominantly reactive, relying on serial monitoring until aneurysms reach intervention thresholds, with surgical or endovascular repair reserved for high-risk cases. This “watchful waiting” approach fails to address the underlying molecular drivers of disease progression and creates substantial physical and psychological burdens for patients. This comprehensive review aims to systematically evaluate the molecular pathogenesis of AAA, with particular focus on identifying and characterizing druggable targets within key signaling pathways governing disease progression. Current management remains predominantly reactive, relying on serial monitoring until aneurysms reach intervention thresholds, with surgical or endovascular repair reserved for high-risk cases. This “watchful waiting” approach fails to address the underlying molecular drivers of disease progression and creates substantial physical and psychological burdens for patients. This comprehensive review aims to systematically evaluate the molecular pathogenesis of AAA, with particular focus on identifying and characterizing druggable targets within key signaling pathways governing disease progression. We will critically assess the pathological roles of pro-aneurysmal pathways (NF-κB, MAPK, STAT, Notch) versus protective signaling cascades (AMPK, PPAR-γ, Nrf2), and elucidate the context-dependent functions of PI3K/Akt and TGF-β pathways. Furthermore, we will examine emerging therapeutic strategies including miRNA-based interventions and nanoparticle-mediated drug delivery systems for their potential to modulate critical pathological processes. By integrating mechanistic insights with therapeutic development, this review aims to establish a conceptual framework for advancing targeted pharmacotherapies that could transform AAA management from surgical intervention to medical prevention, addressing a crucial unmet need in cardiovascular medicine. Risk Factors Male sex and advanced age remain well-established non-modifiable risk factors for AAA. Contemporary population-based imaging studies demonstrate AAA prevalence of 4.0% in men versus 0.7% in women, representing an approximately 5-6-fold higher burden in males. , Recent screening cohorts report even more pronounced disparities, with multivariable-adjusted odds ratios of 8.04 (95% CI 4.87–13.28) for male sex in ultrasound screening studies. Global Burden of Disease analyses indicate that males experience approximately 2.25-fold higher age-standardized death rates from aortic aneurysm compared to females. Age substantially stratifies AAA risk, with peak mortality occurring in men aged 70–74 years and disability-adjusted life years peaking in the 65–69 age group. While women develop AAAs at significantly lower absolute rates, they experience disproportionately worse outcomes: in large US inpatient cohorts, women comprised 22.8% of AAA admissions but rupture accounted for 18.4% of female admissions versus 12.6% of male admissions. Smoking stands as the most potent modifiable risk factor for AAA, profoundly influencing aneurysm formation, progression, and rupture. Large prospective cohorts demonstrate that current smoking confers hazard ratios of 4.32–4.81 for incident AAA compared to never-smokers, with meta-analyses yielding pooled odds ratios of 3.39 (95% CI 2.57–4.48). , , The association exhibits pronounced anatomic specificity: UK Biobank analyses report hazard ratios of 8.90 for abdominal aortic aneurysms and 10.47 for ruptured aortic aneurysms in current versus never-smokers, while thoracic aneurysms show no clear association. Dose-response relationships are evident, with smoking ≥20 versus <10 cigarettes daily associated with HR 5.67 for aortic aneurysm incidence. Pack-year analyses reveal monotonic risk increases: Japanese cohort data show aortic mortality hazard ratios versus never-smokers of 2.39 for <20 pack-years, 3.57 for 20–39 pack-years, and 3.92 for ≥40 pack-years. The smoking effect demonstrates marked sex specificity, with women experiencing disproportionately greater relative risk increases; meta-analyses report a pooled women-to-men relative risk ratio of 1.78 (95% CI 1.32–2.38), indicating current smoking confers 78% greater relative increase in AAA risk in women compared to men. Additionally, factors associated with AAA development include hypertension, atherosclerosis, coronary artery disease, dyslipidemia, cerebrovascular disease, obesity, and a positive family history. Emerging research highlights genetic/epigenetic contributors like microRNAs and lncRNAs. Although diabetes mellitus typically promotes atherosclerosis, type 2 diabetes appears to confer protection against AAA formation. Comprehensive meta-analyses of population and clinical studies demonstrate that diabetic patients have approximately 50% lower AAA risk compared to non-diabetic individuals. Additionally, diabetes is associated with reduced aneurysm expansion rates and markedly decreased rupture risk. , Symptoms Most AAAs typically remain asymptomatic until they rupture, often discovered during routine physical examinations or diagnostic investigations for other health concerns. Patients with unruptured AAAs may occasionally present with vague symptoms, including abdominal discomfort or radiating pain extending to the lumbar region or groin. Larger AAAs can compress nearby structures, such as the ureters, inferior vena cava, or duodenum, potentially leading to symptoms, although this is uncommon. Ischemic symptoms in the lower limbs due to acute thrombosis or embolization of peripheral circulation may occur but are infrequent in AAA patients. Clinical examination may detect a pulsatile epigastric mass on deep abdominal palpation, though this finding has limited diagnostic sensitivity for AAA. Alarmingly, 50% of AAA cases first present with rupture, typically into the retroperitoneal space. This rupture can cause symptoms such as back pain, with or without abdominal pain, hypotension, lightheadedness, and a pulsatile epigastric mass. Diagnosis Imaging is crucial in identifying AAA, monitoring its growth rate, diagnosing rupture, guiding therapeutic decisions, planning treatment, and assessing post-surgical outcomes. Ultrasonography (US) and computed tomography angiography (CTA) are essential for AAA management. Diagnosis Imaging is crucial in identifying AAA, monitoring its growth rate, diagnosing rupture, guiding therapeutic decisions, planning treatment, and assessing post-surgical outcomes. Ultrasonography (US) and computed tomography angiography (CTA) are essential for AAA management. Despite advancements in aortic imaging technologies, ultrasonography remains the preferred method for AAA screening and surveillance due to its wide availability, non-invasive nature, cost-effectiveness, and high diagnostic accuracy. US, including colour and duplex imaging, is indicated for AAA screening and diagnosis in asymptomatic patients and offers rapid emergency assessment for symptomatic cases. For comprehensive characterization and procedural planning, CTA is the cornerstone modality. It provides high-resolution, three-dimensional visualization of the aneurysm’s morphology, including precise measurements of maximum diameter, proximal and distal extension (neck), and involvement of visceral branches. Furthermore, CTA is indispensable for detecting critical features such as the presence of an intraluminal thrombus, penetrating atherosclerotic ulcers, and dissection flaps. This detailed anatomical information is vital for determining eligibility and planning both endovascular (EVAR) and open surgical repair. Consequently, CTA is the definitive test for confirming rupture and for pre-procedural assessment and post-operative surveillance. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) serves as an alternative to CTA, offering advantages such as avoiding radiation exposure and needing iodinated contrast agents. However, MRA is comparatively more expensive, less widely available, and has longer imaging times. Although not part of routine AAA management, positron emission tomography–computed tomography (PET–CT) molecular imaging offers unique diagnostic value for characterizing inflammatory aneurysms, mycotic AAAs, and infected endovascular grafts. Nevertheless, this technique has limitations, including limited spatiotemporal resolution, radiation exposure, high cost, and restricted availability. Treatment Pharmacological Treatment Numerous pharmacological approaches have been explored for potential benefits in the treatment of AAA ( ). However, to date, no medical therapy has proven sufficiently effective in reducing AAA growth or preventing rupture to be incorporated into treatment guidelines. Antihypertensive drugs such as beta-blockers and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors have shown no impact on AAA expansion. , While antibiotics such as doxycycline significantly lowered plasma markers of proteolytic activity, recent studies found no attenuation of AAA expansion. Macrolides (roxithromycin, azithromycin) likewise showed no therapeutic benefit in slowing aneurysm progression. , Although observational data suggest statins may reduce AAA growth rates, larger nonrandomized trials failed to confirm this effect. Other pharmacologic agents including NSAIDs, mast cell inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, diuretics, and angiotensin II receptor blockers demonstrated preclinical potential but ultimately showed no efficacy in curbing AAA enlargement in clinical studies. Current randomized clinical trials are examining the impact of ticagrelor, a platelet aggregation inhibitor; telmisartan/valsartan, an angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB); cyclosporine A, an immunosuppressive agent; and eplerenone, an aldosterone antagonist, on the growth rate of small AAAs. However, there is presently no definitive recommendation for pharmacological intervention to mitigate the risk of AAA progression and rupture. Surgical Treatment Currently, surgical intervention remains the only definitively proven treatment to prevent abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) rupture and associated mortality. The established indications for repair include AAAs reaching 5.5 cm in diameter for male patients or 5.0 cm for female patients, as well as any symptomatic aneurysm regardless of size. For cases where the risks of elective surgery outweigh the potential rupture risk, a conservative approach is recommended. This involves regular monitoring with imaging intervals tailored to aneurysm size: every three years for 3.0–3.9 cm AAAs, annually for 4.0–4.9 cm AAAs, and every 3–6 months for aneurysms ≥5.0 cm, with adjustments made for rapid growth (>1 cm/year) or other high-risk features like elevated wall stress. For smaller AAAs below the surgical threshold, a strategy of surveillance combined with optimal medical management has been shown to be safer and more effective than early elective repair. This comprehensive conservative approach emphasizes rigorous cardiovascular risk factor control, including mandatory smoking cessation, dietary modifications, and regular physical activity. Such lifestyle interventions have demonstrated greater efficacy in reducing cardiovascular events and improving overall outcomes compared to early surgical intervention, while also being cost-effective. The combination of size-appropriate monitoring and aggressive medical therapy represents the standard of care for small AAAs. Currently, two main surgical interventions are employed for AAA repair: open surgical repair (OSR) and endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR). OSR involves a midline laparotomy with replacement of the aneurysmal aortic segment using either a tube or bifurcated synthetic graft, followed by closure of the aneurysm sac around the prosthesis. OSR involves a midline laparotomy with replacement of the aneurysmal aortic segment using either a tube or bifurcated synthetic graft, followed by closure of the aneurysm sac around the prosthesis. This approach carries significant perioperative risks, including cardiac (myocardial infarction), pulmonary (pneumonia), and renal (insufficiency) complications. Postoperative wound complications, particularly incisional hernias following midline laparotomy, significantly impair patient recovery after AAA repair. Potential long-term complications following AAA repair include graft infections, graft limb occlusion, secondary aortoenteric fistulae, and para-anastomotic aneurysm formation. In contrast, EVAR offers a minimally invasive alternative involving percutaneous or open femoral artery access for stent-graft deployment under fluoroscopic guidance after precise angiographic measurements. While EVAR reduces immediate surgical risks, it introduces unique complications, particularly endoleaks and access site issues, especially in patients with challenging iliac anatomy (small, calcified, or tortuous vessels). The choice between these approaches depends on patient anatomy, comorbidities, and surgical expertise. Both surgical interventions are associated with high risk, cost, longer procedural time, severe complications, high mortality rates in unsuccessful procedures, and poor long-term survival. Given the elevated mortality rates associated with rupture and post-surgery, there is a pressing need for alternative pharmacological therapies. Pathogenesis of AAA While the precise pathophysiology of AAA remains incompletely understood, emerging evidence highlights four interconnected pathological processes driving disease progression: (1) dysregulated ECM remodeling, (2) chronic vascular inflammation, (3) immune cell infiltration, and (4) VSMC dysfunction ( ). These processes collectively contribute to structural and biomechanical weakening of the aortic wall in response to hemodynamic stress, aging, and other risk factors. Earlier studies established that AAA development involves both molecular alterations (eg, protease activation, cytokine dysregulation) and mechanical degradation (eg, loss of elastin, collagen disruption). To develop targeted therapies, a deeper investigation of the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying these pathological changes—particularly their role in aortic wall remodeling and rupture risk is critical. Aortic Wall In its normal state, the aorta functions to efficiently transmit pulsatile arterial blood pressure and adapt continually to maintain a consistent diameter in response to changing hemodynamic conditions. This functionality is contingent upon the elastic properties and material composition of the aortic wall. The structural composition of the aortic wall comprises three distinct layers: the tunica intima, tunica media, and tunica adventitia, encompassing the lumen through which blood flow circulates. Each layer serves a specific function and possesses unique mechanical properties. The innermost layer, the intima, directly interfaces with the blood flow. It serves as a selective barrier formed by endothelial cells, preventing blood product infiltration into the wall and facilitating the delivery of oxygen and nutrients from the blood to the inner wall. The middle layer, referred to as the tunica media, represents the thickest vascular layer, measuring ~2 μm distal to the renal arteries. Bounded internally by a prominent internal elastic lamina and externally by a thinner, age-sensitive external elastic lamina, this middle layer consists of concentric elastic lamellae alternating with vascular SMCs. These structural “lamellar units” provide critical circumferential elasticity, protecting against hemodynamic deformation. The media’s extracellular matrix contains sparse fibroblasts within a network of elastin, collagen fibers, proteoglycans, and glycosaminoglycans. The outermost tunica adventitia comprises loose collagen fibers, fibroblasts, neural elements, and vasa vasorum micro vessels, with its collagen framework maintaining structural integrity. ECM The primary component of the blood vessel wall is the ECM, offering structural support to the cells. This dynamic structure is pivotal in governing vascular function, functioning critically under both physiological and pathological circumstances. Maintaining proper ECM function is essential for preserving aortic homeostasis and mechanical properties. The key macromolecules comprising the ECM in large arteries include elastin, collagens, glycoproteins, and proteoglycans, all of which are vital for the function and integrity of the vessel wall. In the middle layer of the aorta, smooth muscle cells are responsible for producing proteins such as elastin and collagen, contributing to the ECM in this part of the aorta. In the adventitia layer, fibroblasts produce collagen, osteopontin, and fibronectin, which are specific to this segment of the aortic wall. Elastin and collagens are the most significant fibrillar proteins in the ECM of the aortic wall, influencing the passive mechanical properties of the aorta. Although vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) retain contractile responsiveness to physiological stimuli and can thereby modulate aortic wall dynamics, this functional capacity appears to have minimal physiological significance in the abdominal aorta’s overall mechanical behavior. Although vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) retain contractile responsiveness to physiological stimuli and can thereby modulate aortic wall dynamics, this functional capacity appears to have minimal physiological significance in the abdominal aorta’s overall mechanical behavior. Elastin Elastin, constituting 50% of the dry weight of the aorta, is a hydrophobic and insoluble protein, serving as the predominant protein in the vascular wall. The ELN gene encodes elastin, and its soluble precursor, tropoelastin, is produced and released into the extracellular space. Tropoelastin monomers undergo polymerization to generate insoluble mature elastin, which then forms a highly cross-linked, rubber-like network through the action of lysyl oxidase, resulting in the development of elastin fibers. Within the middle layer of the aortic wall, elastin fibers are particularly abundant and are peripherally associated with SMCs and collagen fibers, creating lamellar units. Under low tension, the laminae exhibit a wavy configuration, while increased tension causes them to stretch and straighten. Upon tension reduction, the laminae can revert to their original dimensions. Thus, elastin is the primary protein conferring structure to the vascular wall and contributes to elastic recoil in the aorta. Collagen Collagen fibers, the second major structural protein in the aortic wall, constitute approximately 20% of the total protein in the normal aorta. The aortic wall contains various types of collagen, with types I and III being the most abundant, comprising 80–90% of the total collagen. The collagen molecule is composed of three polypeptides twisted together to create a triple helix, and covalent cross-linking between these collagen helices forms large, highly organized fibrillar bundles. Lysyl oxidase (LOX) catalyzes the formation of covalent cross-links between collagen molecules, enabling the assembly of mature collagen fibrils the dominant structural elements of the extracellular matrix. Within the aortic adventitia, this cross-linked collagen network confers critical tensile strength, both protecting against elastin overdistension and providing mechanical resistance to wall deformation. Collagen, being 100–1000 times stiffer than elastin, serves as the load-bearing component at higher pressures, while under normal blood pressure, the stretchy elastic fibers in the middle aortic wall handle the pressure changes. Consequently, elastin fibers and collagen fibrils together create a robust scaffold for the aorta, offering protection against mechanical damage. ECM Remodeling In the vascular wall, remodeling of the ECM is a physiological process essential for maintaining tissue homeostasis and functionality. However, when ECM remodeling becomes excessive or uncontrolled, it can lead to several life-threatening pathological conditions. Abnormal remodeling of the vessel wall diminishes the strength of the aortic wall, and if the forces acting on the aortic wall surpass its strength, it contributes to the development of AAA or leads to rupture. It has been proposed that the rapid fragmentation of elastin fibers may serve as the triggering event in AAA, initiating wall weakening and ultimately causing AAA expansion. Under normal conditions, collagen fibers in the aortic wall remain relaxed. However, as an aneurysm forms and expands, these fibers gradually straighten and align until they approach their maximum stretching capacity. Studies have reported that collagen synthesis increases during the early stages of aneurysm formation, suggesting that collagen turnover is important for vessel wall repair and regeneration and maintaining the strength of the aortic wall and its structural integrity during AAA progression. This suggests that increased collagen synthesis might occur as a response to increased wall tension as a consequence of increased elastin degradation together with an expanding aorta. But in later stages of the disease, collagen degradation exceeds its synthesis, and thus increased degradation of collagen fibers might reduce the mechanical strength of the aortic wall, which in turn becomes the responsible factor for AAA rupture. Thus, as the disease advances, the remodeling of the ECM leads to gradual deterioration and weakening of the aortic wall. This process culminates in dilation and eventual rupture when the aortic wall can no longer endure the hemodynamic forces. Several cellular and molecular mechanisms contribute to ECM remodeling in the progression of AAAs. Among these, proteolysis and inflammation play crucial roles. Normally, MMPs play diverse roles in biological processes, including tissue remodeling, cell growth, proliferation, migration, angiogenesis, vascularization, apoptosis, tissue repair, wound healing, and immune response. All matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) exhibit similar fundamental structural characteristics, consisting of five key domains: a signal peptide that directs protein secretion, an inhibitory propeptide domain that maintains enzyme latency, a catalytic domain responsible for substrate cleavage, a flexible hinge region, and a hemopexin-like domain that contributes to substrate specificity. MMPs are initially secreted in an inactive form known as pro-MMPs, requiring activation for proteolytic activity. The propeptide domain contains a cysteine residue (Cys73), stabilizing the inactive proenzyme. The catalytic domain features an active Zn2+ site bonded to the cysteine residue. The intact Cys73-Zn2+ bond maintains pro-MMP inactivity by preventing water molecules from reacting with the zinc molecule. MMP activation involves disrupting the bond between the active Zn2+ site and the cysteine residue, known as the “cysteine switch”, a conserved mechanism in the MMP family. The elevated activity of these enzymes results in excessive ECM degradation, which contributes to the formation of multiple pathological disease conditions, including the development of AAA. So, it is crucial to control the MMPs’ concentrations in order to regulate the correct level of the proteolytic activity of active MMPs, and One regulatory system involves the endogenous family of tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs). Physiologically, MMP activation is tightly regulated by TIMPs. Aneurysmal tissues often exhibit an imbalance between MMP and TIMP activities, as indicated by messenger RNA level studies. MMP-9, also known as gelatinase B, plays a significant role in elastin, collagen, laminin, gelatin, and fibrinogen degradation. It has been observed that MMP-9 levels and proteolytic activities are upregulated in AAA aortic tissues compared to healthy aortae, and highly correlates with aneurysm size. MMP-9 are highly elevated at the site of aneurysmal rupture, showing AAA rupture is associated with higher levels of MMP-9 in the AAA wall. Furthermore, higher plasma levels of MMP-9 are observed in AAA and aortic dissection patients. Several population-based studies showed that plasma levels of MMP-9 dropped significantly in patients after AAA surgical repair. Moreover, several animal models have been employed to investigate the role of MMP-9 in AAA, and MMP-9-deficient mice exhibit protection against aortic dilation and destruction in experimental aneurysms. In human AAA, histological analysis confirmed that macrophages are the primary source for MMP-9 in the aortic wall, and it is reported that MMP-9 colocalizes with infiltrating macrophages present in the AAA wall mainly in the media and media-adventitia junction. Similar findings are also reported in animal model studies. MMP-9 deficient mice receiving wildtype bone marrow post-nonlethal irradiation showed marked development of AAA, while the converse experiment in which wildtype mice received MMP-9 deficient marrow did not induce aneurysm formation, suggesting macrophage-derived MMP-9 is crucial for AAA formation. Overall, the current opinion regarding MMP-9 is that it is positively related to AAA size, more specifically AAA rupture, and that its causality in AAA is independent of its cellular source and mainly due to inflammatory infiltrate macrophages. MMP-2 is a key protease implicated in the early pathogenesis of abdominal aortic aneurysm, playing a central role in the extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling that drives aneurysm expansion. Primarily produced by vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), MMP-2 exhibits potent elastolytic and gelatinolytic activity, specifically targeting elastin and type IV collagen in the aortic media. While its overall activity levels are generally lower than the inflammation-associated MMP-9 in established aneurysms, increased MMP-2 activity represents an early pathogenic event that precedes significant inflammatory cell infiltration. , Multiple studies in human tissues and animal models consistently demonstrate that elevated MMP-2 activity correlates with characteristic histopathological features of AAA, including elastin fragmentation, collagen disorganization, and progressive aortic dilation. , This evidence positions MMP-2 as a critical initiator of the proteolytic cascade that weakens the aortic wall and facilitates aneurysm development. Although MMPs play a pivotal role in AAA pathogenesis, broad-spectrum MMP inhibition (eg, with doxycycline) has failed to demonstrate clinically meaningful suppression of aneurysm progression in human trials, highlighting the complex interactions and multiple mechanisms involved.
